neocog>lenet.lead: The Neocognitron already had the architecture: local receptive fields, weight sharing across position, and alternating layers of feature detection and pooling. What it did not have was a way to decide what those features should be. LeNet-5 kept the structure and replaced Fukushima's hand-specified learning rule with gradient descent on a task loss, which is the whole of the difference.

blocks.b:
The Neocognitron's S-cells detect a pattern in a small window; the C-cells above them pool the responses of S-cells looking for the same pattern at nearby positions, so a shift in the input moves which S-cell fires but leaves the C-cell response largely unchanged. Stack the pair and tolerance to distortion accumulates layer by layer. Every structural idea a convolutional network relies on is present here.

The weights were another matter. Training was unsupervised and local: a winning cell in a column reinforced its own connections, in the spirit of Hebbian learning, with no reference to whether the network's final answer was right. Nothing propagated backwards. A feature that was useless for the task could be reinforced as readily as a useful one, because the rule had no way to tell the difference.

LeCun's networks kept the receptive fields and the pooling and made the whole stack differentiable, so the same backpropagation that trained a fully connected net could train a convolutional one. Weight sharing is what makes this cheap: a kernel used at every position accumulates one gradient from all of them,

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = \sum_{(i,j)} \frac{\partial L}{\partial y_{ij}} \, x_{i+u,\,j+v}$$

so a layer with thousands of connections has only as many free parameters as one kernel. The constraint is not merely an efficiency trick — it is a statement that a feature worth detecting in one part of the image is worth detecting everywhere, and gradient descent then only has to find that one feature.

LeNet-5 put this to work on digits, with a trained convolutional stack feeding a small classifier, and it was deployed reading cheques at scale. The architecture had stopped being a proposal about biological plausibility and become an engineering result.

blocks.h: What the change cost, and what it postponed
blocks.b:
Backpropagation made the features task-dependent, which is the gain, and simultaneously made the network dependent on labelled data and on compute proportional to the depth. On the digits of the era both were affordable. On natural images neither was, and LeNet-5's design sat almost unchanged for over a decade while the field looked elsewhere.

The pieces that eventually unblocked it were not architectural. ImageNet supplied the labels; GPUs supplied the arithmetic; ReLU and dropout made the deeper stack trainable. When AlexNet arrived it was recognisably LeNet's structure scaled up, which is the strongest evidence that the 1998 design was right and merely early.

Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition

lenet>neocog.lead: This arrow runs backwards in time on purpose. It records that the convolutional network had a fully worked-out ancestor eighteen years before LeNet-5, and that the two differ in exactly one component — how the weights are chosen — rather than in the architecture they share.

blocks.b:
Reading the two designs side by side, the correspondence is nearly term for term. Fukushima's S-cell is a convolution followed by a nonlinearity; his C-cell is a pooling layer; his alternation of S and C layers is the conv-pool stack; his "same feature at many positions" is weight sharing. Hubel and Wiesel's simple and complex cells are the common source both designs cite.

What this means for the genealogy is that the convolutional prior — locality, sharing, and pooling — was not discovered by gradient descent and does not depend on it. It was a hypothesis about the structure of images, stated architecturally, and it survived the change of learning rule intact.

Fukushima's rule is local and label-free, which are genuine advantages: it needs no annotated corpus and no global signal. The cost is that it optimises nothing in particular. Competitive reinforcement will find features that are frequent, and frequency is only loosely related to usefulness for a downstream decision.

The result was a network that handled shifted and mildly distorted digits well and did not obviously improve as it grew. Without an objective there is no gradient to follow, so scale buys little, and the failure is silent — there is no training curve that goes flat, because there is no loss being trained.

Label-free training was not wrong, only premature. What was missing was an objective that a network could optimise without annotations, and the field spent thirty years finding good ones: reconstruct the input, predict a held-out patch, or match two views of the same image.

By the time MAE masks three quarters of an image and asks a ViT to reconstruct it, or ConvNeXt-v2 does the same for a convolutional stack, the ambition is Fukushima's — learn features from unlabelled images — pursued with the tool he lacked. The lineage is not a curiosity: the two ends of it are the same claim, separated by the invention of a differentiable objective.

lenet>alexnet.lead: AlexNet's architecture is LeNet-5's, deeper and wider. What changed was everything around it: a labelled corpus three orders of magnitude larger, two GPUs to run the convolutions, and three training decisions — ReLU, dropout, and heavy augmentation — without which the larger network would not have trained at all.

blocks.h: Why the 1998 design could not simply be scaled
blocks.b:
Enlarging LeNet-5 runs into three walls at once. Saturating nonlinearities are the first: with $\tanh$ or the logistic sigmoid the derivative is near zero across most of its range, so gradient magnitude decays multiplicatively with depth and the early layers barely move. The second is data — a network with tens of millions of parameters fitted to tens of thousands of images memorises them. The third is arithmetic, and it is the hardest, because a convolution over a $224\times224$ image at realistic channel counts is far beyond a 1990s CPU budget.

None of these is an architectural defect. That is the point of the arrow: the design was waiting on its surroundings.

blocks.h: The three changes that made depth trainable
blocks.b:
**ReLU.** $f(x) = \max(0, x)$ has derivative $1$ wherever it is active, so the gradient reaching layer $k$ is not attenuated by a chain of small factors. Krizhevsky et al. report several times faster convergence to a given training error than the $\tanh$ equivalent — an optimisation result, not a representational one.

**Dropout.** Zeroing each unit of the fully connected layers with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$ at training time stops units from co-adapting into brittle detectors, and approximates averaging over an exponential family of thinned networks. The fully connected head held the great majority of AlexNet's weights and was where overfitting actually lived.

**Augmentation.** Random crops and horizontal flips, plus a PCA-based colour jitter, multiply the effective corpus at negligible cost and encode the invariances the task is known to have.

blocks.h: What it settled, and what it left untidy
blocks.b:
AlexNet roughly halved the top-5 error of the best entry of the previous ImageNet competition, and it did so with a learned end-to-end pipeline against hand-engineered descriptors with a trained classifier on top. That single result moved the field's default from feature design to architecture design, and it is the reason nearly every arrow in this lane after 2012 exists.

The network itself is not a clean object. The $11\times11$ first-layer kernels, the stride, and the split across two GPUs are artefacts of a 3 GB memory limit rather than principles, and the fully connected head carries most of the parameters for a small share of the work. ZFNet's visualisations diagnosed the first of those within a year, and VGG replaced the large kernels outright.

alexnet>zfnet.lead: AlexNet worked and nobody could say why. Zeiler and Fergus built a way to project a given activation back into pixel space, looked at what the first two layers had actually learned, found two concrete defects in the kernel size and stride, and fixed them. It is the point at which architecture tuning stopped being guesswork.

blocks.h: Projecting an activation back to pixels
blocks.b:
The deconvnet attaches to a trained network and runs it in reverse. To see what drives one feature map, all other activations in that layer are zeroed and the remaining signal is passed back down: unpooling using the **switches** recorded at pooling time, so each value returns to the location it came from; rectification, so the reconstructed signal stays positive; then the transposed filters of the forward pass.

The switches are what make this more than a gradient picture. Max pooling is not invertible, and without a record of which position won, the back-projection would smear the response over the whole window. Storing the argmax makes the reconstruction sharp enough to read.

Two faults were visible immediately. The first-layer filters were a mixture of extremely high-frequency and very low-frequency structure with little in between — a sign that $11\times11$ kernels were covering too much at once. And the second layer showed aliasing artefacts, which traced to the stride of $4$ in the first convolution skipping over information.

The fix was to reduce the first-layer kernels to $7\times7$ and the stride to $2$. Both are small numbers. Both were reached by looking rather than by search, and the retuned network beat AlexNet on ImageNet.

The immediate accuracy gain matters less than the method. ZFNet established that a convolutional network is inspectable, that its failures leave visible signatures, and that a hypothesis about a hyperparameter can be tested by looking at what the layer learned rather than by running the whole training grid.

The same paper's occlusion experiments — slide a grey square over the image and watch the class probability fall — became the standard way to ask which pixels a decision depends on, and are the ancestor of the saliency and attribution literature. What ZFNet does not provide is a new architecture; it is a diagnosis, and the architectures that acted on it are VGG and everything after.

zfnet>vgg.lead: ZFNet had shown that AlexNet's large first-layer kernels were the wrong shape. VGG took the conclusion to its limit: use only $3\times3$ convolutions, stack them, and let depth rather than kernel size supply the receptive field. It is the cleanest controlled experiment in the lane — one variable, depth, moved at a time.

blocks.h: Why a stack of small kernels is the better buy
blocks.b:
Three $3\times3$ convolutions in series see a $7\times7$ region, the same as one $7\times7$ convolution. The parameter counts differ. For $C$ channels in and out, the stack costs $3 \times (3^2 C^2) = 27C^2$ weights against $7^2 C^2 = 49C^2$ for the single large kernel — around $45\%$ fewer.

And the stack passes through three nonlinearities instead of one, so it can express functions the single layer cannot. Fewer parameters and a strictly richer function class is not a trade-off; it is a straight win, which is why the $3\times3$ kernel became the default for the next decade of convolutional design.

Simonyan and Zisserman's real contribution is methodological. They fix the kernel size, the stride, the pooling, and the channel-doubling schedule, and then vary only the number of layers, reporting a family from 11 to 19 weight layers. Accuracy improves monotonically over that range, which is the result the field needed: depth, holding everything else fixed, is what helps.

The uniformity had a second effect nobody planned. Because every VGG stage has the same shape, features could be lifted out of it and reused, and for several years VGG was the default backbone for detection, segmentation and style transfer — a role its successors inherited only by matching that regularity.

blocks.h: The bill, in the fully connected head
blocks.b:
VGG-16 carries roughly $138$ million parameters and the great majority sit in the three fully connected layers at the end, with the first of them alone — $7 \times 7 \times 512$ inputs to $4096$ units — accounting for over a hundred million. The convolutional trunk that does the actual visual work is a small fraction of the total.

That imbalance is what GoogLeNet attacks with $1\times1$ bottlenecks and global average pooling in place of the dense head. The compute bill is separate and just as heavy: VGG-19's forward pass costs an order of magnitude more arithmetic than AlexNet's, and depth beyond about 19 layers stopped helping — a wall that had nothing to do with kernel size and needed the residual connection to break.

refs.t: Very Deep Convolutional Networks for Large-Scale Image Recognition

vgg>googlenet.lead: VGG bought accuracy with parameters, most of them in a dense head doing little visual work. GoogLeNet asked what could be had at a fixed budget instead, and answered with two moves: a $1\times1$ convolution that reduces channel depth before any expensive kernel runs, and global average pooling in place of the fully connected classifier.

blocks.b:
A $1\times1$ convolution has no spatial extent; it is a learned linear map across channels applied at every position. Placed before a $3\times3$ or $5\times5$ kernel it cuts the channel count that kernel has to consume, and the saving is multiplicative.

For $C_{\text{in}} = 256$ channels into a $5\times5$ convolution producing $C_{\text{out}} = 128$, the direct cost per position is $5^2 \times 256 \times 128 \approx 819\mathrm{K}$ multiply-accumulates. Reducing to $64$ channels first costs $256 \times 64 = 16\mathrm{K}$ and leaves $5^2 \times 64 \times 128 \approx 205\mathrm{K}$ — under a third of the original, for one extra layer.

The Inception module spends the saving on width: parallel $1\times1$, $3\times3$, $5\times5$ and pooling branches, concatenated, so one block sees several scales at once instead of committing to a kernel size.

The second economy is blunter. Instead of flattening the final feature map into fully connected layers, GoogLeNet averages each channel over its spatial extent, producing one number per channel, and classifies from that. A $7\times7\times1024$ map becomes a $1024$-vector with no parameters at all.

VGG-16's first dense layer alone holds more weights than the whole of GoogLeNet, which lands near $6.8$ million parameters against VGG's $138$ million while scoring better on ImageNet. Global average pooling also removes the fixed input-size constraint the flatten imposed, and acts as a structural regulariser: each channel is pushed towards being a class-relevant detector rather than an arbitrary coordinate.

blocks.h: What it bought and what it cost
blocks.b:
GoogLeNet won ILSVRC 2014 with roughly twenty times fewer parameters than the VGG entry it beat, which permanently separated "parameter count" from "accuracy" as design targets and made efficiency a first-class axis. The $1\times1$ bottleneck it introduced is now everywhere — ResNet's bottleneck block, MobileNet's pointwise stage, and every inverted residual since.

The cost is legibility. The branch widths, the reduction ratios and the placement of the auxiliary classifiers were tuned by hand and do not follow from anything, so the design transfers poorly: changing the input resolution or the class count leaves no principled way to adjust it. Inception-v3 rationalised the topology, and the search-based lineage from NASNet onwards eventually replaced hand-tuning altogether.

vgg>resnet.lead: VGG had shown accuracy improving with depth up to 19 layers. Past that it reversed, and not from overfitting — the deeper network was worse on the training set. ResNet identified that as an optimisation failure and removed it by changing what each block is asked to learn: a residual from its input rather than a fresh function of it.

blocks.b:
He et al. give the diagnostic that makes the problem tractable. A 56-layer plain network has higher **training** error than a 20-layer one. Overfitting would show as low training error and high test error, so that is not what is happening.

The argument from construction is what makes it damning. Take the shallow network and append layers that compute the identity; the result is a deeper network with exactly the shallow one's error. A solution of at least that quality therefore exists in the deeper hypothesis class, and gradient descent is not reaching it. The failure is in the optimiser's ability to find the solution, not in the class's ability to contain it.

If the useful thing for a block to do is stay near the identity, make the identity free. A residual block computes

$$y = \mathcal{F}(x, \{W_i\}) + x$$

so the stacked layers only have to produce the **difference** between input and desired output. Driving $\mathcal{F}$ to zero is easy — push the weights towards zero, which is where initialisation and weight decay already point — whereas driving a stack of nonlinear layers to reproduce its input exactly is not.

The backward pass shows the second effect. Differentiating through the sum gives $\partial y / \partial x = 1 + \partial \mathcal{F} / \partial x$, so every block passes gradient through unattenuated regardless of what its weights are doing. The identity path is a route by which the loss reaches early layers without being multiplied by a long chain of Jacobians.

blocks.h: What it unlocked, and what it did not fix
blocks.b:
Depth stopped being the binding constraint. ResNet-152 trains stably and wins ILSVRC 2015, and the paper reports a 1202-layer variant that optimises without difficulty, if without benefit. The skip connection then propagated out of vision entirely — the Transformer's sublayers, U-Net's decoder, and essentially every deep architecture since carry one.

What depth did not deliver was proportionate return. Beyond about 100 layers accuracy flattens, and the reason is not optimisation any more: Wide ResNet shows that many deep-and-thin blocks contribute little, and buys the same accuracy from far fewer, wider ones. The receptive field also grows only slowly with depth, which is what pushed later work towards larger kernels and attention.

refs.t: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
Identity Mappings in Deep Residual Networks

googlenet>resnet.lead: The residual connection is ResNet's own idea, but the block it is wrapped around is GoogLeNet's. ResNet's deeper variants spend their budget through a $1\times1$ reduce, $3\times3$ process, $1\times1$ restore sandwich — the Inception bottleneck, applied in series rather than in parallel.

blocks.b:
ResNet-50 and above replace the two $3\times3$ layers of the basic block with three: a $1\times1$ that cuts channel depth, a $3\times3$ at the reduced width, and a $1\times1$ that restores it. For a block operating on $256$ channels and reducing to $64$, the expensive middle convolution costs $3^2 \times 64 \times 64$ multiply-accumulates instead of $3^2 \times 256 \times 256$ — a factor of sixteen, for two cheap projections either side.

That is precisely the arithmetic GoogLeNet used to afford its parallel branches. ResNet keeps the economy and drops the parallelism, which is what makes it uniform enough to scale by simply repeating a stage.

ResNet ends the way GoogLeNet does: no flatten, no dense head, just an average over the spatial extent of the final feature map into a single linear classifier. VGG's hundred-million-parameter head does not reappear anywhere in the residual family.

Combined with the bottleneck, this is why ResNet-50's parameter count lands around $25$ million — a sixth of VGG-16's — while being both deeper and more accurate. The residual connection gets the credit for the depth; the Inception-derived economies are what kept that depth affordable.

The exchange did not stop. Inception-v4 and Inception-ResNet run the traffic the other way, putting residual shortcuts inside Inception blocks and finding the same acceleration in training that ResNet reported. ResNeXt then reads the Inception module as a special case: replace the hand-designed heterogeneous branches with many identical ones, and the branch count becomes a clean scaling axis.

What survives from GoogLeNet is therefore not the module but the two economies underneath it. The $1\times1$ bottleneck and the parameterless classifier head are in almost every backbone in this lane, including the ones that abandoned convolution.

Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

resnet>residual.lead: ResNet introduced the identity shortcut to solve a specific problem in a specific place — degradation in very deep convolutional stacks on ImageNet. Within two years the same connection was load-bearing in architectures that share nothing else with it. This arrow marks the point where a block became a technique.

blocks.h: What generalised out of the block
blocks.b:
Strip ResNet's convolutions away and what remains is a rule about composition: when stacking transformations, add the input back. Written as $y = \mathcal{F}(x) + x$, nothing in it refers to images, kernels, or spatial structure. $\mathcal{F}$ can be anything differentiable.

Two properties travel with it. The gradient through the sum is $1 + \partial\mathcal{F}/\partial x$, so depth no longer attenuates the signal reaching early layers, and the zero function — not the identity — becomes the easy thing for the block to learn, which is what makes a near-identity layer reachable by gradient descent.

The Transformer wraps every sublayer in one: attention and feed-forward alike are $x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(\mathrm{LN}(x))$, and without it the deep stacks that language models are built from do not train. U-Net's decoder, the diffusion U-Net, the residual blocks inside VAEs and GANs, and graph networks all carry the same construction.

A companion paper made the placement precise. **Identity Mappings in Deep Residual Networks** shows that keeping the shortcut path clean — moving normalisation and activation into the residual branch rather than after the addition — gives an unbroken multiplicative-free route from any layer to any deeper one, and it is that pre-activation ordering that most later architectures adopted.

The shortcut makes depth trainable, not useful. Wide ResNet's result is that many of the deep-and-thin blocks a residual network affords contribute very little, and comparable accuracy is available from far fewer, wider ones — so "1000 layers train fine" and "1000 layers help" are different claims, and only the first is true.

There is a reading of residual networks as ensembles of relatively shallow paths, which explains both the trainability and the diminishing return: adding depth mostly adds more short paths rather than genuinely deeper computation. And the identity path is not free at run time — it forces the block's input and output to have matching shape, which is why every stage transition needs a projection, and it holds an extra activation tensor in memory for the backward pass.

resnet>densenet.lead: ResNet adds a block's input to its output. DenseNet concatenates instead, and gives every layer in a block direct access to the output of every layer before it. The change is one operator, and it converts the shortcut from a gradient highway into an explicit feature-reuse mechanism.

blocks.b:
In a residual block the identity and the transformed signal are summed, so the two are combined into one tensor and cannot be separated again. Whatever the earlier layer computed is available downstream only in whatever mixture the addition produced.

DenseNet's layer $\ell$ instead receives the concatenation of every preceding feature map in its block:

$$x_\ell = H_\ell\big([x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_{\ell-1}]\big)$$

so a feature computed at layer 2 is still individually addressable at layer 20. A block of $L$ layers has $L(L+1)/2$ connections rather than $L$, and each layer decides for itself which of the earlier features it wants.

blocks.h: Why this makes the network thinner, not fatter
blocks.b:
The counter-intuitive result is that concatenation reduces the parameter count. Because earlier features are preserved rather than recomputed, each layer only needs to contribute a small number of new maps — the **growth rate** $k$, typically 12 or 32 — instead of producing a full-width output.

A DenseNet layer is therefore very narrow, and the paper reports competitive ImageNet accuracy at roughly half the parameters of a comparable ResNet. Transition layers with $1\times1$ convolutions and pooling sit between blocks to stop the concatenated width growing without bound. Every layer also has a short path to the loss, which sharpens the implicit deep supervision the residual connection already provided.

Parameter efficiency and memory efficiency are not the same thing, and DenseNet trades one for the other. A naive implementation materialises the concatenated tensor at every layer, so activation memory grows quadratically with block depth even though the weights do not. Training a large DenseNet was memory-bound long before it was compute-bound.

The fix is to recompute concatenations in the backward pass rather than store them, which trades arithmetic for memory and is what the efficient implementations do. Even so the access pattern is awkward for hardware that prefers dense contiguous tensors, and CSPNet later attacked exactly this: split the stage, send only half through the dense connections, and concatenate at the end, keeping most of the reuse at a fraction of the traffic.

Memory-Efficient Implementation of DenseNets

resnet>resnext.lead: Depth and width were the two knobs a residual network offered, and both had started to give diminishing returns. ResNeXt adds a third — **cardinality**, the number of parallel transformation branches inside a block — and reports that at fixed complexity, raising it beats raising either of the others.

blocks.h: Split, transform, merge, with identical branches
blocks.b:
Inception blocks split a signal across several branches, transform each differently, and concatenate. Their weakness is that every branch's kernel size and width is set by hand, so the design does not transfer between stages or datasets.

ResNeXt keeps the topology and makes the branches identical. A block aggregates $C$ transformations of the same form:

$$y = x + \sum_{i=1}^{C} \mathcal{T}_i(x)$$

where every $\mathcal{T}_i$ is the same bottleneck shape with its own weights. There is nothing left to hand-tune but the count $C$, and because the branches are homogeneous the whole aggregate is exactly a grouped convolution — one kernel with its channels partitioned into $C$ groups that do not mix.

The paper's discipline is holding complexity fixed. ResNeXt-50 with $32$ groups of width $4$ carries essentially the same parameter count and FLOP count as ResNet-50, and improves ImageNet top-1 by roughly a point and a half — and ResNeXt-101 in the same configuration reaches accuracy the authors compare to a ResNet twice its depth.

Raising cardinality while shrinking branch width therefore buys more than raising depth or width at the same budget. The interpretation the paper offers is that many low-dimensional embeddings aggregated together are a better use of a fixed parameter count than one high-dimensional one.

blocks.h: What the hardware thinks of it
blocks.b:
The theoretical FLOP count is unchanged; the achieved throughput is not. Grouped convolution partitions the channel dimension, which is the dimension GPU kernels most want contiguous and dense. A $32$-group convolution is $32$ narrow matrix multiplications rather than one wide one, and narrow matrix multiplications leave tensor units idle.

So ResNeXt is a case where FLOPs mislead — the same problem MnasNet later attacked from the search side by putting measured latency into the objective. The idea survived regardless: grouped and depthwise convolution became standard, ResNeSt added attention within the groups, and the extreme case where the group count equals the channel count is the depthwise convolution the whole efficiency lineage is built on.

refs.t: Aggregated Residual Transformations for Deep Neural Networks

resnet>wrn.lead: Residual connections made a thousand layers trainable, and ResNet's own results showed the return on them collapsing well before that. Zagoruyko and Komodakis tested the other direction: keep the residual block, cut the depth by an order of magnitude, multiply the width, and measure. The shallow wide network wins on both accuracy and wall-clock time.

blocks.h: Diminishing returns, and a reason for them
blocks.b:
ResNet-1001 improves on ResNet-100 by very little for ten times the depth. The explanation the paper offers is **diminishing feature reuse**: with a residual block free to approximate the identity, gradient descent has no pressure to make every block do work, so a long stack contains many blocks that learn almost nothing and merely pass their input along.

Depth is then partly wasted capacity, and worse, it is sequential — layer $k+1$ cannot start until layer $k$ finishes, so depth costs latency that no amount of parallel hardware recovers.

blocks.h: Width, and dropout put back inside the block
blocks.b:
A widening factor $k$ multiplies the channel count of every convolution in the residual blocks. WRN-28-10 — 28 layers, ten times ResNet's width — outperforms the thousand-layer ResNet on CIFAR while training several times faster in wall-clock terms, because wide layers are large dense matrix multiplications and that is what GPUs are built to do.

The second finding is that the widened network overfits without help, and that the help has to go in the right place: dropout **between the convolutions inside a residual block**, on the residual branch, not on the identity path. Batch normalisation alone was not sufficient regularisation once the blocks were wide.

blocks.h: The cost, and where it left the field
blocks.b:
Parameters grow with the square of the width, since a convolution's weight count is proportional to $C_{\text{in}} \times C_{\text{out}}$. WRN-28-10 is a large model by the standards of its year, and the memory that width consumes is the reason the trade is not universally favourable — on memory-constrained targets the deep thin network is still the affordable one.

What the paper established is that depth, width and resolution are separate axes with separate returns, and that picking one and pushing it is arbitrary. EfficientNet's compound scaling is the direct answer: rather than argue about which axis to favour, scale all three together by a fixed ratio found once by search.

refs.t: Wide Residual Networks

resnet>senet.lead: A convolution mixes channels with weights fixed after training, so the relative importance of feature channels is the same for every image the network ever sees. Squeeze-and-Excitation makes that mixture input-dependent: pool each channel to a single number, learn a gate from those numbers, and rescale the channels before passing them on.

blocks.b:
The block is three operations on a feature map $U \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}$. **Squeeze** collapses each channel to a scalar by global average pooling,

$$z_c = \frac{1}{H W} \sum_{i=1}^{H} \sum_{j=1}^{W} u_c(i, j)$$

giving every channel a receptive field covering the whole image regardless of its kernel size. **Excite** passes $z$ through a two-layer bottleneck, $s = \sigma\big(W_2\,\delta(W_1 z)\big)$, where $\delta$ is ReLU and the reduction ratio $r$ — 16 in the paper — sets the hidden width. **Scale** multiplies each channel by its gate: $\tilde{u}_c = s_c\, u_c$.

The parameter cost is roughly $2C^2/r$ per block, a low single-digit percentage of a ResNet, and the block drops into an existing architecture without changing anything around it.

blocks.h: Why a scalar per channel is enough
blocks.b:
The gate is a $C$-vector, not a spatial map, which is what keeps it cheap and also what makes it a statement about *which features matter here* rather than *where they are*. If an image is of a beach, channels tuned to sand and water should be amplified and channels tuned to fur suppressed, everywhere in the image at once.

SENet won ILSVRC 2017 and the block was retrofitted to ResNet, ResNeXt and Inception with a consistent gain in each. Its more lasting effect is architectural: it made *attention as a cheap reweighting module* a standard component, and MobileNet-v3, EfficientNet and the whole NAS-designed efficiency family include it by default.

Global average pooling reduces $H \times W$ values to one, so all spatial structure is gone before the gate is computed. A channel that matters intensely in one corner and not at all elsewhere gets a single scalar decision applied uniformly, and the block has no way to express the distinction.

That gap is what the immediate successors fill from different directions. CBAM adds a spatial attention map alongside the channel one; SKNet lets the gate choose between branches with different kernel sizes, so the receptive field itself becomes input-dependent; ResNeSt applies the same reweighting within feature-map groups rather than across the whole width. The block also introduces a sequential dependency — the whole map must be pooled before any of it can be scaled — which is a synchronisation point in an otherwise streaming convolution and part of why SE blocks cost more latency than their FLOP count suggests.

refs.t: Squeeze-and-Excitation Networks

googlenet>inceptionv3.lead: GoogLeNet worked but read as a pile of choices nobody could justify. Inception-v3 is the paper that goes back and states the design principles, then applies them systematically — factorising every large kernel, fixing the grid-reduction bottleneck, and adding label smoothing.

blocks.b:
Two substitutions do most of the work. A $5\times5$ convolution is replaced by two stacked $3\times3$ convolutions, which cover the same region for roughly $\tfrac{18}{25}$ of the arithmetic — VGG's argument, applied inside Inception.

The second goes further: an $n \times n$ convolution becomes an $n \times 1$ followed by a $1 \times n$. For $n = 7$ that is $14$ multiply-accumulates per channel pair against $49$, a saving of about $70\%$. The paper is careful about where this works — asymmetric factorisation helps on medium-sized grids, roughly $12$ to $20$ across, and does not pay off early in the network.

blocks.h: The representational bottleneck, and label smoothing
blocks.b:
The stated principle is to avoid representational bottlenecks: do not reduce spatial size and channel width in a way that forces the signal through a narrow point, because information lost there cannot be recovered by any later layer. Applied to grid reduction, this replaces the naive pool-then-convolve with parallel strided convolution and pooling branches whose outputs are concatenated, so the width expands as the resolution halves.

Label smoothing is the other durable contribution. Instead of a one-hot target, the correct class gets $1 - \epsilon$ and the remaining mass is spread across the others. A one-hot target is only reached by driving the correct logit to infinity, so it pushes the network towards overconfidence; smoothing bounds that and improves calibration. It has been standard in classification training ever since, well outside Inception.

blocks.h: What was fixed and what was not
blocks.b:
Inception-v3 reaches substantially better ImageNet accuracy than GoogLeNet at a comparable order of compute, and it is the version that stayed in service for years as a general-purpose feature extractor and as the backbone of the FID metric that generative models are still scored with.

What it did not achieve is simplicity. The topology is still a hand-assembled catalogue of module variants at different stages, and the paper's principles constrain the design without determining it. Two lines follow from that dissatisfaction: Inception-ResNet adds residual shortcuts to make the deep version trainable faster, and Xception pushes the factorisation to its limit by asking what happens when spatial and cross-channel correlation are decoupled entirely.

refs.t: Rethinking the Inception Architecture for Computer Vision

inceptionv3>inceptionv4.lead: Inception-v3 had reached the limit of what hand-tuning could add. Inception-ResNet keeps its factorised modules and threads a residual shortcut through each one, and the result is not better final accuracy so much as markedly faster convergence — with one stability problem that needed a fix of its own.

blocks.b:
The modification is mechanical. Each Inception module's concatenated branch output is passed through a $1\times1$ convolution to match the input width, then added to the input rather than carried forward alone. The branch structure, the factorised $n\times1$ and $1\times n$ kernels, and the grid-reduction blocks are all Inception-v3's.

The paper reports that the residual variants reach a given accuracy in substantially fewer epochs than the equivalent non-residual Inception-v4. On final accuracy the two are close, which is the more interesting result: the shortcut is buying optimisation speed here, not representational power. Inception blocks were already wide enough that gradient flow, not capacity, was the binding constraint.

Training the wide residual variants failed at scale in a specific way: with more than roughly a thousand filters, the network died early in training — the last layer before the average pooling began producing zeros after a few tens of thousands of iterations, and lowering the learning rate or adding extra normalisation did not prevent it.

The fix is to scale the residual branch down before the addition, by a constant in the region of $0.1$ to $0.3$:

$$y = x + \alpha \, \mathcal{F}(x), \qquad \alpha \approx 0.1 \text{–} 0.3$$

This keeps the identity path dominant early in training so the block starts near an identity map and grows its contribution as the weights become useful. The same trick — scale the residual branch, or initialise its last layer to zero — reappears throughout later deep architectures, which is a sign it was addressing something general rather than an Inception quirk.

blocks.h: The end of the hand-designed line
blocks.b:
Inception-ResNet-v2 was among the strongest ImageNet models of its moment, and it is effectively the last of its kind. The topology has dozens of hand-chosen branch widths and module counts, and there is no principle left that says why any of them takes the value it does.

What replaced that process is search. NASNet, appearing the same year, spends compute rather than human judgement on the same question and produces cells that beat Inception's by the paper's own comparison — and the efficiency lineage from MnasNet onwards then adds device latency to the objective. The Inception idea itself survives in a narrower form: InceptionNeXt revives parallel multi-scale branches, but inside a single depthwise kernel of a ConvNeXt block rather than as a whole architecture.

refs.t: Inception-v4, Inception-ResNet and the Impact of Residual Connections on Learning

resnet>inceptionv4.lead: This is the return leg of the exchange between the two dominant backbone families. ResNet had already borrowed GoogLeNet's $1\times1$ bottleneck; here the identity shortcut travels the other way, into the Inception modules, and the paper that does it is explicitly a test of how much the residual connection is worth on its own.

blocks.h: The experiment the paper is actually running
blocks.b:
Szegedy et al. build two families deliberately: Inception-v4, a pure non-residual architecture with the branch structure cleaned up and made uniform, and Inception-ResNet, the same lineage with shortcuts added. Training both under matched conditions isolates the shortcut as a variable.

The answer is that residual connections accelerate training considerably and do not, by themselves, raise the ceiling — Inception-v4 without any shortcut reaches comparable accuracy given enough epochs. That is a sharper claim than ResNet's own paper could make, because ResNet's plain baseline was degrading rather than merely slow, and it locates the shortcut's contribution in optimisation.

A residual connection requires the branch output and the input to have the same width, which an Inception module's concatenated output does not, so each block gains a $1\times1$ projection whose only job is to restore the shape. Inside the residual variants the branches are also simplified relative to v4 — batch normalisation is dropped from the summation path to keep memory affordable.

And then the wide-filter instability appears, requiring the residual branch to be scaled by roughly $0.1$–$0.3$ before adding. Fitting a shortcut to a heterogeneous multi-branch block is therefore not free; ResNet's own blocks are uniform precisely so that the shape always matches.

The paper's best reported result is an ensemble of Inception-v4 and three Inception-ResNet-v2 models, which reached the strongest ImageNet top-5 numbers of its moment. That the two families ensemble well is itself informative: the errors they make are different enough to be worth averaging, so the hand-designed multi-branch topology and the uniform residual stack were finding partly different features.

After this the two lines stop converging and both give way. Grouped and depthwise convolution replace hand-set branches, search replaces hand-set widths, and by the time ConvNeXt reconstructs a convolutional backbone from first principles it starts from ResNet's uniformity rather than Inception's variety — while borrowing the large-kernel and inverted-bottleneck ideas that Inception's factorisation work had first raised.

refs.t: Inception-v4, Inception-ResNet and the Impact of Residual Connections on Learning
Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

senet>sknet.lead: Squeeze-and-Excitation lets a network decide which channels matter for a given image. SKNet asks the next question — how large a region each neuron should look at — and answers it the same way: run branches with different kernel sizes, then learn a soft, input-dependent choice between them.

blocks.h: Making the receptive field a variable
blocks.b:
In a standard convolutional stack the receptive field at every depth is fixed once the kernel sizes and strides are chosen. A neuron that needs broad context for one image and fine detail for another has no way to express that; the architecture has already decided.

SKNet runs the input through parallel branches with different effective kernel sizes — a $3\times3$ and a $5\times5$, the latter implemented as a dilated $3\times3$ to keep the cost down — and combines them with weights the network computes from the input itself. The receptive field becomes a learned function of what is being looked at.

The branch outputs are summed and squeezed exactly as in SE: global average pooling to a channel vector, then a bottleneck to a compact descriptor $z$. Where SE emits one gate, SKNet emits one per branch and normalises **across branches** with a softmax, so for channel $c$ with branch logits $a_c, b_c$,

$$s_c = \frac{e^{a_c}}{e^{a_c} + e^{b_c}}, \qquad V_c = s_c\,\tilde{U}_c + (1 - s_c)\,\hat{U}_c$$

The softmax is the whole difference. SE's sigmoid gates each channel independently — every channel can be on, or all off. SKNet's gates compete, so the block must **allocate** attention between receptive-field sizes rather than merely scale them, and the paper's analysis shows the selected size growing for targets that occupy more of the frame.

Multiple branches mean the block computes the feature map more than once, and the dilated implementation reduces but does not remove that. SKNet is more expensive per block than an SE-equipped ResNeXt of similar accuracy, and it sits in the awkward region where the gain is real but the cost is hard to justify against simply widening the network.

Its idea nonetheless kept moving. ResNeSt takes the same softmax-across-branches construction and applies it across feature-map **groups** rather than kernel sizes, which is cheaper and composes with the grouped convolution that was already standard. And the general point — that receptive-field size should be data-dependent — is what self-attention provides natively, which is part of why the vision transformers made this particular line of convolutional work less pressing.

refs.t: Selective Kernel Networks
Squeeze-and-Excitation Networks

resnext>resnest.lead: ResNeXt established that a residual block should be many parallel branches rather than one wide one, and then treated those branches as interchangeable — their outputs are simply summed. ResNeSt keeps the split and replaces the sum with a learned, input-dependent weighting across the branches.

blocks.b:
ResNeXt has a single structural parameter, the cardinality $K$. ResNeSt adds a second: within each of the $K$ groups the features are split again into $R$ **radix** splits, giving $K \times R$ sub-groups in total.

The cardinality splits behave as they do in ResNeXt. The radix splits are what attention is computed over. Inside a group, the $R$ splits are summed to form a descriptor, global average pooling reduces it to a channel vector, and a bottleneck produces $R$ sets of weights normalised by a softmax across the splits — so the group's output is a convex combination of its own sub-branches rather than a plain sum.

The distinction from SE is where the attention is computed. SE pools the entire feature map and emits one gate per channel for the whole width; ResNeSt computes its statistics **within each cardinality group**, so a group specialising in one kind of structure makes its own decision without being averaged against groups doing something else.

This is also why the block composes cheaply. The grouped convolution is already there for ResNeXt's sake; split-attention adds only the small pooling-and-bottleneck path per group, so the construction rides on machinery the architecture was paying for anyway. Stacked into a ResNet-50 layout, ResNeSt-50 reports a substantial ImageNet gain over ResNeXt-50 at broadly comparable cost, and larger gains again on the dense-prediction tasks that use it as a backbone.

blocks.h: How much is the block and how much is the recipe
blocks.b:
ResNeSt arrived with a training setup that had itself improved markedly since ResNeXt: large-batch schedules, label smoothing, mixup, auto-augmentation, cosine learning-rate decay and dropblock. Several of the reported gains would appear for a plain ResNet trained the same way, and the paper's own ablations are the place to look rather than the headline number.

That ambiguity is not unique to ResNeSt — it is the reason ConvNeXt's methodology, holding the training recipe fixed while modernising one architectural element at a time, was received as it was. What is not in doubt is that ResNeSt became a strong detection and segmentation backbone, and that its split-attention block is the closest the grouped-convolution line came to the input-dependent mixing that attention provides directly.

refs.t: ResNeSt: Split-Attention Networks
Aggregated Residual Transformations for Deep Neural Networks

senet>resnest.lead: ResNeSt's split-attention is squeeze-and-excitation with its scope narrowed. The three steps are SENet's — pool, bottleneck, gate — but they run inside each feature-map group and normalise across splits rather than across the whole width, which is what lets channel attention coexist with grouped convolution.

blocks.b:
SE pools a feature map over its spatial extent to a channel vector, passes it through a two-layer bottleneck with reduction ratio $r$, and uses the result to rescale the channels. Split-attention performs exactly that sequence — global pooling, bottleneck, gate — and differs only in what it pools over and how the gate is normalised.

Inherited wholesale is the central claim: a scalar summary per channel carries enough information to decide that channel's importance for this input. Everything ResNeSt does rests on SE having established that a $C$-vector gate is worth its parameters.

blocks.h: Sigmoid across channels, softmax across splits
blocks.b:
SE's gate is $\sigma(\cdot)$ applied per channel, so the gates are independent — a block may amplify everything or suppress everything. ResNeSt's is a softmax over the $R$ radix splits of a group, so the weights for a given channel sum to one across splits.

Independent gating **scales**; competitive gating **selects**. The softmax form comes directly from SKNet, which used it to choose between kernel sizes; ResNeSt applies the same normalisation to feature-map groups instead, where the splits are cheaper to produce because grouped convolution is already computing them.

A plain SE block sits outside the group structure: it pools the whole width, so a single statistic is shared by groups that may be doing unrelated work, and the gate cannot distinguish them. Applying SE to a ResNeXt therefore leaves most of what cardinality bought unexploited.

Running the attention per group closes that gap, and it is the last significant refinement of the channel-attention line in this lane. What follows is not a better gate but a different mechanism — self-attention computes an input-dependent mixture over spatial positions as well as channels, without a hand-placed pooling step — and ConvNeXt's finding that a well-tuned convolutional stack needs no attention block at all to match a Swin Transformer is the other half of the same conclusion.

densenet>cspnet.lead: DenseNet's concatenation gives every layer access to every earlier feature, and in doing so makes many layers receive nearly the same gradient. CSPNet splits the stage in two, routes only one half through the dense connections, and concatenates at the end — keeping most of the reuse while cutting the duplicated work.

blocks.b:
In a dense block, layer $\ell$ sees $[x_0, \ldots, x_{\ell-1}]$ and every subsequent layer sees those same maps again. During the backward pass each of those layers sends gradient back through the same early features, so a large fraction of the gradient arriving at $x_0$ is repeated information rather than new signal.

The consequence is that the network spends parameters and memory learning transformations that are highly correlated with each other. The dense connectivity that makes DenseNet parameter-efficient in one sense makes it computationally redundant in another.

CSPNet partitions the stage's input feature map along the channel dimension into $x' $ and $x''$. Only $x''$ passes through the dense block; $x'$ bypasses it entirely and is concatenated with the block's output before a transition layer merges the two.

Because the bypassed half never enters the dense connections, the gradient paths through the two halves are different, and the duplication is broken by construction rather than by regularisation. The paper reports around a $20\%$ reduction in computation on an equivalent backbone with accuracy maintained or improved, and — because the split halves the width entering the expensive block — a corresponding drop in peak memory traffic.

CSPNet is deliberately not a network. It is a transformation applied to an existing stage, and the paper demonstrates it on DenseNet and ResNeXt alike, producing CSPDenseNet and CSPResNeXt. That makes its contribution portable and its identity dependent on the host.

Its real career was in detection, where memory bandwidth on mid-range hardware is the binding constraint. YOLOv4 adopted a CSP backbone, and the CSP block stayed in the YOLO line through subsequent versions — which is why an idea framed as a fix for DenseNet's gradient redundancy is now best known as a standard component of real-time detectors.

refs.t: CSPNet: A New Backbone that can Enhance Learning Capability of CNN
Densely Connected Convolutional Networks

googlenet>xception.lead: An Inception module splits a signal into branches that look at channels and space in different mixtures. Chollet's reading is that the module is an interpolation between two extremes, and that the hypothesis behind it — cross-channel and spatial correlations can be mapped separately — is worth taking to the limit rather than tuned in the middle.

blocks.b:
A standard convolution maps spatial and cross-channel correlations jointly: one kernel of shape $D_K \times D_K \times M$ produces each output channel by mixing all input channels across a spatial window in a single operation.

Inception's $1\times1$ branches do the cross-channel part first and the spatial part second, on a subset of channels at a time. Chollet observes that this is a point on a spectrum whose extreme is one spatial kernel per channel with no mixing at all, followed by a $1\times1$ that does all the mixing — the **depthwise separable** convolution. If the decoupling hypothesis is right, the extreme should be the best point, and Xception is the test.

The arithmetic strongly favours it. A standard convolution costs $D_K^2 \cdot M \cdot N \cdot D_F^2$ multiply-accumulates; the separable version costs $D_K^2 \cdot M \cdot D_F^2 + M \cdot N \cdot D_F^2$, and the ratio is

$$\frac{1}{N} + \frac{1}{D_K^2}$$

For a $3\times3$ kernel and any realistic output width $N$, that is close to $\tfrac{1}{9}$. Xception spends the saving on width and depth instead of banking it, arriving at roughly the same parameter count as Inception-v3 — around $23$ million — and reporting slightly better ImageNet accuracy with a clearly larger margin on the far bigger JFT dataset.

Two details differ from the MobileNet form that followed. Xception applies the $1\times1$ before the depthwise stage, and it places no nonlinearity between them; the paper's ablation finds that inserting one **hurts**, which is a hint about narrow intermediate representations that MobileNet-v2 later made precise.

Because the saving was reinvested, Xception is not a cheap model — it matches Inception-v3's budget and beats it on accuracy, which is the intended result. The efficiency reading of depthwise separable convolution belongs to MobileNet, which took the same primitive and kept the saving.

The practical catch is that FLOPs and speed diverge here. A depthwise convolution performs very little arithmetic per byte of memory it touches, so it is bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound, and hardware built for dense matrix multiplication runs it far below peak. That gap between theoretical cost and measured latency is exactly what MnasNet was built to measure, and what MobileNet-v4 is still negotiating with.

refs.t: Xception: Deep Learning with Depthwise Separable Convolutions
Going Deeper with Convolutions

xception>mobilenet.lead: Xception showed that depthwise separable convolution matches a full convolution's accuracy at a fraction of the arithmetic, and spent the saving on a bigger model. MobileNet keeps it, and adds two multipliers that let a single architecture be dialled down to whatever budget the target device actually has.

blocks.b:
The primitive is the same: a depthwise convolution applies one spatial kernel per input channel with no mixing, and a following $1\times1$ pointwise convolution does all the cross-channel combination. The cost ratio against a standard convolution is $\tfrac{1}{N} + \tfrac{1}{D_K^2}$, roughly $\tfrac{1}{9}$ for $3\times3$ kernels.

Where Xception reinvested that factor in depth and width, MobileNet banks it. The result is a network of around $4.2$ million parameters and well under a billion multiply-accumulates that lands within a couple of points of VGG-16 on ImageNet — a model that fits on a phone rather than one that wins a competition. MobileNet also places batch normalisation and ReLU after **both** the depthwise and the pointwise stage, unlike Xception's unbroken pairing.

The multipliers are what make it deployable. The **width multiplier** $\alpha$ scales every layer's channel count, so cost falls roughly as $\alpha^2$; the **resolution multiplier** $\rho$ scales the input image, and cost falls roughly as $\rho^2$ again. Together,

$$\text{cost} \;\approx\; \alpha^2 \rho^2 \left( D_K^2 M D_F^2 + M N D_F^2 \right)$$

The paper reports the whole trade-off curve rather than one operating point, so an engineer with a fixed latency target can read off the configuration instead of designing a new network. That framing — one family, parameterised by budget — is the template every mobile architecture since has followed, and it is the direct ancestor of EfficientNet's compound scaling, which asks what the *right* joint setting of these knobs is instead of leaving them independent.

Shrinking $\alpha$ makes the layers narrow, and narrow layers with ReLU on them lose information irrecoverably — a rectifier on a low-dimensional representation collapses part of it to zero with no way back. That is the failure MobileNet-v2's linear bottleneck was built to fix, and it is why aggressive width reduction cost more accuracy than the FLOP saving suggested.

The multipliers are also set by hand, which means the shape of the network is uniform even though the hardware's preferences are not: some layers are bandwidth-bound, others compute-bound, and one global $\alpha$ cannot express that. Filling that gap is the whole point of the search-based line — MnasNet putting measured latency in the reward, and MobileNet-v3 letting the search choose the layout per platform.

refs.t: MobileNets: Efficient Convolutional Neural Networks for Mobile Vision Applications
Xception: Deep Learning with Depthwise Separable Convolutions

mobilenet>mbv2.lead: MobileNet lost accuracy faster than it lost FLOPs when the width multiplier was turned down, and the reason was the rectifier. MobileNet-v2 diagnoses it — ReLU on a narrow layer destroys information permanently — and restructures the block around that: expand first, keep the nonlinearity in the wide part, and leave the narrow bottleneck linear.

blocks.h: What ReLU does to a narrow layer
blocks.b:
Sandler et al. make the argument with a direct experiment: embed a low-dimensional manifold into $\mathbb{R}^n$ by a random matrix, apply ReLU, and try to invert it. For small $n$ the reconstruction is badly corrupted; for large $n$ it is close to exact.

The reason is that ReLU is information-preserving only on the part of the input where it is linear. If the representation occupies a low-dimensional subspace, zeroing the negative orthant collapses a substantial share of it, and no later layer can recover what was set to zero. In a wide layer the manifold of interest is likely to survive somewhere in the active region; in a narrow one it is not.

The conclusion is uncomfortable for MobileNet-v1, whose whole efficiency strategy is making layers narrow and then applying ReLU to them.

A ResNet bottleneck goes wide → narrow → wide, with the shortcut connecting the wide ends. MobileNet-v2 inverts it: narrow → wide → narrow, with the shortcut connecting the **narrow** ends.

A block takes a thin tensor, expands it by a factor $t$ (typically $6$) with a $1\times1$, applies the depthwise $3\times3$ and ReLU6 in that expanded space where the nonlinearity is safe, then projects back down with a $1\times1$ that has **no activation** — the linear bottleneck. The residual connects the two thin tensors.

Both halves matter. The nonlinearity now lives where the representation is high-dimensional enough to survive it, and the residual carries the thin tensor, which is the cheap thing to add and to keep in memory.

The parameter count and the FLOP count both fall relative to v1 at equal accuracy, and MobileNet-v2 became the standard mobile backbone almost immediately — it is also the block MnasNet, MobileNet-v3 and EfficientNet all search over rather than replace.

The cost is transient activation memory. The expanded tensor is $t$ times the width of the block's input and output, so a naive implementation holds a large intermediate for every block even though nothing outside the block ever sees it. The paper's answer is that the expansion never has to be materialised in full: because the $1\times1$ operates per position, the block can be evaluated in channel-wise chunks, trading a little arithmetic for a much smaller peak footprint. That optimisation is why the design is deployable on hardware where total memory, not FLOPs, is the wall.

refs.t: MobileNetV2: Inverted Residuals and Linear Bottlenecks

mbv2>mbv3.lead: MobileNet-v2's block was right and the numbers around it — how many blocks, how wide, where to spend the budget — were still chosen by hand. MobileNet-v3 hands that to a search that optimises measured latency on a specific phone, then applies a small set of hand fixes to the parts the search handles badly.

blocks.b:
The architecture is produced in two passes. Platform-aware NAS, in the form MnasNet established, searches the global block layout against a reward combining accuracy with latency measured on the target device. **NetAdapt** then runs a fine-grained pass that trims individual layers' channel counts one at a time, keeping whichever trim costs the least accuracy per millisecond saved.

The division of labour is the point. Coarse search decides the skeleton; the layer-wise pass tunes the widths, which is where uniform multipliers like MobileNet-v1's $\alpha$ were leaving the most on the table. The output is two models, Large and Small, aimed at different points on the latency curve rather than one architecture with a knob.

blocks.h: Hard-swish, and where the search is wrong
blocks.b:
The swish nonlinearity $x \cdot \sigma(x)$ improves accuracy but is expensive on mobile hardware, so v3 substitutes a piecewise-linear approximation:

$$\mathrm{h\text{-}swish}(x) = x \, \frac{\mathrm{ReLU6}(x + 3)}{6}$$

which needs no exponential and reuses the ReLU6 already in the pipeline. It is applied only in the deeper half of the network, where the feature maps are small enough that the cost is negligible. Squeeze-and-excitation blocks are included in some stages, with the gate's sigmoid replaced by its hard variant for the same reason.

The hand fixes are at the two ends, which is where a latency-driven search reliably misjudges. The stem is cut from $32$ filters to $16$, and the expensive final stages are restructured — the last expansion is moved past the average pooling so it runs on a $1\times1$ spatial grid instead of $7\times7$. The paper attributes several milliseconds to that one rearrangement.

blocks.h: What a searched architecture does not transfer
blocks.b:
The result is faster than MobileNet-v2 at higher accuracy on the device it was searched for, and the qualifier carries weight. The reward function contains a latency table for one platform; a different accelerator with different preferences about depthwise convolution, channel alignment or activation cost will not rank the same candidates the same way.

So each new target implies a new search, at a cost measured in device-hours, and the architecture ages as the hardware does. MobileNet-v4's universal inverted bottleneck is the response — a single block family parameterised so that one architecture can be tuned across accelerators rather than re-searched for each — and its own limitation is the same one, deferred.

NetAdapt: Platform-Aware Neural Network Adaptation for Mobile Applications
MnasNet: Platform-Aware Neural Architecture Search for Mobile

resnet>nasnet.lead: ResNet, Inception and their descendants were assembled by people making judgement calls that no principle determined. NASNet replaces the judgement with search — but searching a whole network is intractable, so its real contribution is finding a unit small enough to search and general enough to stack.

blocks.h: Searching a cell, not a network
blocks.b:
The insight that makes the problem tractable is that hand-designed backbones already repeat themselves. ResNet is a stage repeated; Inception is a module repeated. So the search space is not the network but the **cell**, and NASNet defines two: a *normal cell* that preserves spatial resolution and a *reduction cell* that halves it.

A controller — a recurrent network trained by reinforcement learning, with validation accuracy of the trained child model as the reward — emits a cell as a sequence of choices: which two earlier outputs to take, which operation to apply to each from a fixed menu of convolutions, separable convolutions and poolings, and how to combine them.

The architecture is then built by stacking the discovered cells, and depth and width become free parameters of deployment rather than of search. Searching on CIFAR-10 and transferring the cell to ImageNet is what keeps the cost survivable, and the transfer working at all is the paper's central empirical claim.

blocks.h: What it found, and what it cost
blocks.b:
The searched cells beat the hand-designed families of the time on ImageNet at comparable cost, and the paper introduced ScheduledDropPath — dropping whole paths in the cell with a probability that rises during training — as the regularisation the discovered topologies needed.

The bill is the headline objection. The search consumed compute on the order of thousands of GPU-days, which put it beyond nearly everyone and made each individual result unreproducible in practice. It also optimises accuracy alone: nothing in the reward knows that a separable convolution with an awkward channel count may be slow on real hardware regardless of its FLOP count.

blocks.h: The two objections that shaped what came next
blocks.b:
Both were answered directly. MnasNet puts **measured latency on a target device** into the reward, so the search optimises the quantity that is actually deployed against, and adopts a factorised search space that allows different blocks in different stages instead of one repeated cell. The cost objection produced weight sharing and differentiable relaxations — ENAS and DARTS — which brought search from thousands of GPU-days towards single-digit ones.

What NASNet established regardless is the framing everything after inherits: define a small repeated unit, search it against an explicit objective, and stack the winner. EfficientNet's baseline comes from exactly this kind of search, and its contribution is the scaling rule applied on top rather than the cell itself.

refs.t: Learning Transferable Architectures for Scalable Image Recognition
Neural Architecture Search with Reinforcement Learning
DARTS: Differentiable Architecture Search

nasnet>mnasnet.lead: NASNet searched for accuracy and used FLOPs as the stand-in for cost. On a phone, FLOPs and milliseconds are not proportional — depthwise convolutions are bandwidth-bound, some channel counts stall the accelerator. MnasNet puts a stopwatch in the reward loop and searches against the number that matters.

blocks.b:
Rather than constrain the search to a FLOP budget, MnasNet optimises accuracy and latency jointly, with a soft weighting that lets the search trade between them:

$$\max_{m}\; \mathrm{ACC}(m) \times \left[\frac{\mathrm{LAT}(m)}{T}\right]^{w}$$

where $T$ is the target latency and $w$ is negative, so exceeding $T$ is penalised smoothly instead of being ruled out. A model comfortably under budget is rewarded for spending the slack on accuracy.

The critical detail is that $\mathrm{LAT}(m)$ is **measured by running the candidate on a real phone**, not estimated. Every proxy the field had been using — FLOPs, parameter count, layer count — mispredicts on hardware whose bottleneck is memory traffic rather than arithmetic.

The second change follows from the first. NASNet searches one cell and repeats it, which implicitly assumes the right structure is the same at every resolution. Latency measurement shows that it is not: an operation that is cheap on a $7\times7$ grid with many channels can be ruinous on a $112\times112$ grid with few.

MnasNet therefore uses a **factorised hierarchical** search space — the network is divided into stages, and each stage's block type, kernel size, squeeze-excitation ratio, layer count and width are searched separately. The space is large enough to express genuinely heterogeneous networks and structured enough to stay searchable, and the discovered models do come out non-uniform in exactly the way the latency data predicts.

MnasNet reported models faster than MobileNet-v2 at higher ImageNet accuracy on the phone they were searched for, and the methodology became standard: MobileNet-v3 uses this search as its first pass, and EfficientNet's B0 baseline comes from the same multi-objective family with FLOPs restored as the target.

The limitation is stated in the reward itself. $\mathrm{LAT}$ is a function of one device, one runtime and one set of kernels; change any of them and the ranking moves. Each new target costs another search — thousands of device-hours — and a model tuned for last year's accelerator is not automatically good on this year's. That treadmill is what MobileNet-v4 set out to get off, by looking for a block family that is Pareto-optimal across accelerators rather than optimal on one.

Learning Transferable Architectures for Scalable Image Recognition

mnasnet>efficientnet.lead: Given a good small network, the field enlarged it by picking an axis — more layers, more channels, bigger inputs — and pushing. EfficientNet's claim is that the axes are not independent, that there is a fixed ratio in which they should be raised together, and that one grid search is enough to find it for a whole family.

blocks.b:
Each axis saturates on its own, and for a legible reason. Depth alone runs into vanishing returns even with residual connections — Wide ResNet's finding. Width alone gives wide but shallow networks that capture fine detail and struggle with high-level structure. Resolution alone feeds more pixels to a receptive field too small to use them.

The interaction is the point. A higher-resolution input needs more layers to grow the receptive field to cover it, and more channels to represent the finer patterns now visible. Scaling one while holding the others fixed spends capacity where it cannot be used.

EfficientNet parameterises all three by one coefficient $\phi$:

$$d = \alpha^{\phi}, \qquad w = \beta^{\phi}, \qquad r = \gamma^{\phi}, \qquad \text{subject to}\quad \alpha \cdot \beta^{2} \cdot \gamma^{2} \approx 2$$

The constraint is dimensional. Convolutional cost is linear in depth but quadratic in both width and resolution, so that product is what fixes the FLOP increase at roughly $2^{\phi}$ — the user picks $\phi$ from a compute budget and the shape follows.

$\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are found once by a small grid search on the baseline and then held fixed. The baseline itself, EfficientNet-B0, comes from a multi-objective search in MnasNet's mould, so the lineage is direct: MnasNet supplies the network worth scaling, and EfficientNet supplies the rule for scaling it. B0 through B7 are the same architecture at $\phi = 0 \ldots 7$, and B7 reached the strongest ImageNet accuracy of its moment with roughly an order of magnitude fewer parameters than the models it displaced.

blocks.h: What the rule does not model
blocks.b:
The scaling law is about FLOPs, and FLOPs are again the wrong currency in two places. Training memory grows with resolution faster than the rule accounts for, so the large variants need small batches and become slow to train — the specific complaint EfficientNetV2 was written to answer, along with the observation that depthwise convolutions are poorly served by accelerators in the early high-resolution stages.

The coefficients are also fitted once, on one baseline, at small scale, and assumed to hold across the whole family. Later work found that the best ratios drift with model size and with the training recipe, and that much of B0-to-B7's reported advantage narrows when the baselines are trained with modern augmentation and schedules — the same recipe-versus-architecture confound that runs through this whole period of the lane.

mnasnet>mbv3.lead: MobileNet-v3 does not invent its search; it takes MnasNet's, whole. The platform-aware reward and the factorised stage-wise space are reused as the first of two passes, and what v3 adds is a finer second pass and a short list of hand corrections where the search misjudges.

blocks.b:
The coarse pass is MnasNet's multi-objective search: candidate architectures are trained, run on the target phone, and scored by accuracy weighted against measured latency. The block vocabulary is the MobileNet-v2 inverted residual with optional squeeze-and-excitation, and stages may differ from one another.

Nothing in that description is new to v3. What it establishes is that the searched-for skeleton is a solved sub-problem, and that the remaining gains are elsewhere — in per-layer widths, in the choice of nonlinearity, and at the two ends of the network.

blocks.h: NetAdapt, and the ends of the network
blocks.b:
The second pass is layer-wise. NetAdapt proposes small reductions to individual layers' channel counts, measures each against the latency table, and keeps whichever gives the best accuracy-per-millisecond, repeating until the budget is met. Coarse search picks the shape; this picks the widths, which is where a global multiplier like MobileNet-v1's $\alpha$ was crudest.

The hand corrections are at the stem and the head, and they are instructive because they are where latency-driven search reliably goes wrong. The first convolution is cut from $32$ filters to $16$ with no accuracy loss. The final expansion stage is moved to **after** the global average pooling, so it runs on a $1\times1$ grid rather than a $7\times7$ one — the same computation, several milliseconds cheaper, and not a move the search space could express.

blocks.h: Cheap nonlinearities, and the standing bill
blocks.b:
Swish, $x\,\sigma(x)$, is accurate and expensive; v3 substitutes $\mathrm{h\text{-}swish}(x) = x \cdot \mathrm{ReLU6}(x+3)/6$, which needs no exponential, and applies it only in the deeper stages where the grids are small. The sigmoid inside the squeeze-excitation gate gets the same hard treatment.

What carries over unchanged from MnasNet is the dependence on one device. Both passes consult a latency table for a specific phone and runtime, so the architecture is optimal against that measurement and nothing else. Reaching a new accelerator means re-running the search rather than adapting the model, which is the constraint MobileNet-v4's universal block was designed to relax.

NetAdapt: Platform-Aware Neural Network Adaptation for Mobile Applications

senet>efficientnet.lead: EfficientNet's contribution is the scaling rule, not the block. The block is MobileNet-v2's inverted residual with a squeeze-and-excitation module inside it — SENet's, adopted without modification, and by then standard enough in searched architectures that its presence goes almost unremarked.

blocks.b:
An EfficientNet block expands its input by a factor $t$ with a $1\times1$, applies a depthwise convolution, passes the result through a squeeze-and-excitation gate, then projects back down linearly with the residual joining the narrow ends. Everything but the gate is MobileNet-v2.

The SE module is the standard three steps: global average pooling to a channel vector, a two-layer bottleneck, a sigmoid, and a per-channel rescale. Its parameter cost is a small fraction of the block, which is precisely why a searched architecture keeps it — under a reward that weighs accuracy against latency, a cheap module with a consistent accuracy gain always survives.

blocks.h: Why a depthwise stack wants channel attention
blocks.b:
There is a structural reason the pairing works better here than in a plain ResNet. Depthwise convolution deliberately removes cross-channel mixing from the spatial stage — that is the whole source of its efficiency — leaving all channel interaction to the $1\times1$ layers, which are position-wise and linear.

Squeeze-and-excitation restores a cross-channel interaction of a different kind: one that is global in space and conditioned on the input. In an architecture built from separable primitives, that fills a gap the design created, which is why SE blocks are near-universal in the efficiency lineage — MnasNet's search space, MobileNet-v3, EfficientNet and EfficientNetV2 all carry them — and comparatively optional elsewhere.

blocks.h: The latency the FLOP count hides
blocks.b:
The gate is nearly free in arithmetic and not free in time. Global average pooling is a reduction over the whole spatial extent, so every value must be produced before any output can be scaled — a synchronisation barrier in the middle of an otherwise streaming pipeline, and a poor fit for accelerators that want to keep data moving.

That is one of several places where EfficientNet's FLOP-optimal family runs slower than its numbers promise, alongside depthwise convolutions in the high-resolution early stages and the memory cost of large input resolutions. EfficientNetV2's response is to replace the depthwise stages early in the network with fused ones and to make the search itself training-aware, which trims exactly these gaps between the theoretical cost model and the clock.
