The implementation matters because the naive version is wasteful. Shifting produces partial windows at the edges, so a batch would contain windows of several sizes. Swin instead cyclically rolls the feature map, keeps every window full-sized, and masks the attention logits between regions that the roll made adjacent but that are not actually neighbours. The batch stays regular and no compute is spent on padding.

Patch merging concatenates $2 \times 2$ neighbouring patches and projects them, halving the resolution and doubling the width at each stage. The result is a stride-4 through stride-32 hierarchy — precisely the interface that FPN necks, detection heads and segmentation decoders were built against, so Swin drops into existing dense-prediction systems where ViT could not.

Position is handled differently too. ViT adds a learned absolute embedding to each token; Swin adds a learned **relative position bias** $B$ inside the attention computation,

$$\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}} + B\right)V$$

indexed by the offset between two tokens within a window. Relative encoding is the right prior for images — what matters is that one patch is two to the left of another, not its absolute coordinate — and the paper's ablation shows it clearly beating the absolute form.

Swin took the state of the art on COCO detection and ADE20K segmentation, not only ImageNet, and became the default transformer backbone for dense prediction.

It is worth naming what was traded. Locality and a resolution hierarchy are exactly the convolutional inductive biases ViT set out to discard; Swin's result is that vision wants them, and that the productive move was hybridisation rather than purity. ConvNeXt then makes the symmetric argument — take a ResNet, apply Swin's macro design and training recipe, and match it with no attention at all — which together suggest the gains of this period belonged more to the design and training conventions than to the attention operator. Swin's own residue is a set of hand-chosen constants: window size, shift amount, and a relative-position table that has to be interpolated when the resolution changes, which is one of the problems Swin-v2 was written to fix.

refs.t: Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows
An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale

swin>swin2.lead: Scaling Swin up exposed two failures that are invisible at ordinary size: activations that grow without bound through the residual stream until training diverges, and a position encoding that has to be interpolated whenever the window changes, which is exactly what transferring to a higher resolution requires.

blocks.b:
Swin follows the pre-norm convention — normalise, transform, add — so the residual stream accumulates the raw output of every block. At large depth and width the activation amplitude at the deep layers was found to be orders of magnitude greater than at the shallow ones, and training collapsed.

**Res-post-norm** moves the layer normalisation to the *end* of each residual branch, after the attention or MLP and before the addition. Every contribution entering the stream is normalised, so the accumulation is bounded by construction and the discrepancy between shallow and deep activations largely disappears.

blocks.h: Cosine attention, and a learned position function
blocks.b:
The second instability is in attention itself. With dot-product logits, a few token pairs can dominate the softmax when the embedding norms grow, so the map collapses onto a handful of positions. **Scaled cosine attention** removes the magnitude:

$$\mathrm{Sim}(q_i, k_j) = \frac{\cos(q_i, k_j)}{\tau} + B_{ij}$$

with $\tau$ learnable. Logits are bounded regardless of how large the embeddings become, which makes the block behave the same at any scale.

For position, the fixed bias table is replaced by a small MLP mapping a relative offset to a bias, with the offsets taken on a **log scale**. Because it is a continuous function rather than a lookup, a window size never seen in training is evaluated rather than interpolated — and the log spacing means a large change in resolution is a small change in input to the MLP, so transfer from a low-resolution pretraining to a high-resolution fine-tune extrapolates gently.

Together these carried Swin to around three billion parameters and images of $1536 \times 1536$, with results across classification, detection and segmentation, plus memory work — activation checkpointing, a sequential self-attention implementation and ZeRO-style optimiser sharding — without which the model does not fit regardless of stability.

The fixes are corrective rather than conceptual: the architecture is Swin's, made to survive its own scaling. And the model at that size needs a corpus and a cluster to match, so SwinV2-G is a demonstration of the ceiling rather than something most people run. The self-supervised pretraining used to feed it, SimMIM, is arguably the more portable half of the work.

refs.t: Swin Transformer V2: Scaling Up Capacity and Resolution
SimMIM: A Simple Framework for Masked Image Modeling

vit>cvt.lead: ViT cuts an image into non-overlapping patches with a linear projection and then relies on attention to discover that neighbouring patches are related. CvT puts convolutions back in two places — the token embedding and the query-key-value projection — and finds that the position embedding becomes unnecessary as a result.

blocks.b:
ViT's patchify step is a stride-$P$ convolution with kernel $P$: the patches do not overlap, so a feature straddling a boundary is split between two tokens that share no input pixels.

CvT replaces it with an overlapping convolution, applied not once but at the start of each of three stages, with stride greater than one so the token count falls and the channel width rises. That gives the model two things at once — local continuity, since adjacent tokens now see overlapping regions, and a resolution hierarchy of the kind Swin builds with patch merging.

blocks.h: Convolutional projection, and dropping the position embedding
blocks.b:
The second change is inside the attention block. Instead of projecting tokens to $Q$, $K$ and $V$ with a position-wise linear map, CvT reshapes the token sequence back to a 2-D grid and applies a **depthwise separable convolution** to produce them.

The query projection uses stride 1; the key and value projections use stride 2, which subsamples them and cuts the attention cost roughly fourfold with little accuracy loss — the same spatial-reduction bargain PvT makes, arrived at through convolution.

The consequence the paper emphasises is that CvT needs **no positional encoding at all**. Convolution is not permutation-invariant: its output at a position depends on where its inputs sit relative to one another, so spatial structure enters the tokens directly. Removing the position embedding also removes the interpolation problem when the input resolution changes — the model transfers to a new size without any surgery.

CvT reports strong ImageNet accuracy with fewer parameters and FLOPs than comparable ViT and DeiT models, and the ablations attribute the gains to the two convolutional insertions separately.

The honest reading is that it puts back what ViT removed. Locality, translation behaviour and hierarchy are convolutional inductive biases, and CvT's result is that a transformer trained on ImageNet-scale data wants them — the same conclusion Swin, PvT and the rest of the hybrid line reached by different routes, and the one ConvNeXt pressed to its logical end by asking whether the attention was contributing anything the design and recipe were not. The depthwise convolution also reintroduces a memory-bound operation into a block that was otherwise dense matrix multiplication, which costs latency the FLOP count does not show.

refs.t: CvT: Introducing Convolutions to Vision Transformers
An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale

vit>pvt.lead: ViT emits one sequence at one scale, which is the wrong interface for detection and segmentation and too expensive to run at their resolutions. PvT builds a four-stage pyramid of shrinking token grids and cuts attention's cost by reducing what the keys and values are computed over — a different route to the same destination as Swin's windows.

blocks.b:
The network is divided into four stages, each beginning with a patch-embedding step that reduces the token grid and widens the channels. The first stage works at stride 4 — far finer than ViT's stride 16 — and the last at stride 32.

The fine first stage is the point. Detecting small objects requires features at high resolution, and ViT's stride-16 tokenisation discards that before the first layer runs. Producing a stride-4 to stride-32 hierarchy means PvT can be dropped straight into an FPN-based detector in place of a ResNet, which the paper demonstrates with RetinaNet and Mask R-CNN, and it was among the first transformer backbones shown to work that way.

A stride-4 grid is enormous — over three thousand tokens at $224 \times 224$, and vastly more at detection resolutions — so full attention is impossible. SRA reduces the key and value sequences before attending:

$$\mathrm{SRA}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{Attention}\big(Q,\; \mathrm{Reshape}(K, R)W_K,\; \mathrm{Reshape}(V, R)W_V\big)$$

where a reduction ratio $R$ collapses each $R \times R$ neighbourhood of the key-value grid into one token via reshape and linear projection. Cost falls by a factor of $R^2$, and $R$ is set largest in the early high-resolution stages where it is most needed.

Queries are left at full resolution, so every position still receives its own output. The difference from Swin is what is given up: Swin restricts *which* tokens interact and keeps them at full detail; PvT keeps global interaction and coarsens what is attended to.

blocks.h: Still quadratic, and still cutting patches apart
blocks.b:
The reduction lowers the constant but not the order — attention remains quadratic in the token count, since only the key-value side shrinks. At the resolutions detection actually uses, the first stage stays expensive.

Two more weaknesses carry over from ViT. The patch embeddings are non-overlapping, so local continuity is broken at every stage boundary. And the model still uses a fixed-size position embedding that must be interpolated when the input resolution changes, which is routine in detection. PvT-v2 addresses all three: pooling to a fixed-size key-value grid makes the attention genuinely linear, overlapping patch embedding restores continuity, and a depthwise convolution inside the feed-forward block supplies position implicitly so the embedding can be removed.

refs.t: Pyramid Vision Transformer: A Versatile Backbone for Dense Prediction without Convolutions
Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows

pvt>pvt2.lead: PvT's three loose ends were a spatial reduction that lowered attention's constant without changing its order, non-overlapping patch embeddings that severed local continuity, and a position embedding that needed interpolating at every new resolution. PvT-v2 closes all three, each with one small change.

blocks.h: Linear attention by pooling to a fixed size
blocks.b:
SRA divides the key-value grid by a fixed ratio $R$, so its size still grows with the input and the attention cost still grows quadratically. **Linear SRA** instead adaptively pools the key-value grid to a **constant** $P \times P$ — the paper uses $P = 7$ — regardless of input resolution.

With the key-value side fixed, attention cost becomes $O(hw \cdot P^2)$, linear in the number of queries. A detector at $800 \times 1333$ now pays proportionally to its token count rather than to its square, which is what makes the backbone practical at the resolutions dense prediction actually uses.

blocks.h: Overlapping patches, and convolution in the feed-forward
blocks.b:
Patch embedding becomes an overlapping convolution — larger kernel, smaller stride, with padding — so adjacent tokens share input pixels and a feature spanning a boundary is no longer split between two tokens that never saw each other's pixels.

The feed-forward block gains a $3 \times 3$ **depthwise convolution** between its two linear layers, applied after reshaping the tokens back to a grid. This does two jobs. It supplies local mixing inside a block that was otherwise entirely position-wise. And because convolution is sensitive to arrangement, it encodes position implicitly, so the explicit position embedding can be deleted — which removes the interpolation step whenever the resolution changes, and lets one set of weights serve any input size.

Zero padding in these convolutions is doing more work than it appears: it is what lets a token near the border infer that it is near the border, which is the mechanism by which convolution conveys absolute position at all.

PvT-v2 improves markedly on v1 across classification, detection and segmentation, and became a common backbone in dense-prediction systems — SegFormer's encoder is built on the same ideas.

The pooled key-value grid is a real approximation, not a free lunch. Collapsing an entire feature map to $7 \times 7$ before attending discards fine spatial distinctions among keys, and the loss is greatest exactly where the reduction ratio is largest — the early high-resolution stages. The architecture also ends up, like CvT and every other member of this family, reinstating convolution inside a design whose original claim was that convolution was dispensable.

refs.t: PVTv2: Improved Baselines with Pyramid Vision Transformer
Pyramid Vision Transformer: A Versatile Backbone for Dense Prediction without Convolutions

vit>crossvit.lead: ViT fixes one patch size, and that single number decides a trade the model cannot revisit: small patches give fine detail at quadratic cost, large patches give cheap global structure and lose the detail. CrossViT runs both and lets the two branches exchange information through their class tokens.

blocks.b:
A small-patch branch produces a long sequence with fine granularity; a large-patch branch produces a short one covering the same image coarsely. The branches are not symmetric — the paper gives the large-patch branch more width and depth, since its sequence is short and capacity there is cheap, while the small-patch branch is kept narrow because its sequence is long.

Each branch runs several transformer blocks independently, and they are fused periodically rather than at every layer. What this buys over one branch at an intermediate patch size is that the two representations are genuinely different in kind, and the fusion has something to combine.

The obvious fusion — attention between all tokens of both branches — costs the product of the two sequence lengths, which defeats the purpose. CrossViT's mechanism is to treat each branch's **class token as its agent**.

The class token from one branch is inserted into the other branch's patch sequence and attends over it, acting as the query while that branch's patches supply keys and values. It gathers what it needs, is projected back, and rejoins its own branch. Since only a single token crosses over, the cost is linear in sequence length rather than quadratic.

The design leans on the class token already serving as each branch's summary — it is the vector the classifier reads — so using it as the carrier between branches is asking it to do a job it is already shaped for.

CrossViT improves on DeiT at comparable FLOPs, with the ablations showing the cross-attention fusion clearly better than concatenating or averaging the branches.

The architecture is nonetheless heavier and more intricate than a single tower: two branches must be sized and balanced, the fusion frequency is another hyperparameter, and the memory footprint reflects both sequences. The problem it addresses — that one patch size cannot serve every scale — is also solved more economically by a hierarchy, which is what Swin and PvT provide by construction, and multi-scale in that form became the dominant answer. What CrossViT retains is the cleanest demonstration that a light, token-level exchange is enough to fuse two representations, without dense attention between them.

refs.t: CrossViT: Cross-Attention Multi-Scale Vision Transformer for Image Classification
Training data-efficient image transformers & distillation through attention

swin>maxvit.lead: Swin made attention affordable by confining it to a window, and paid for that with locality: information crosses between windows only gradually, shift by shift. MaxViT keeps window attention and adds a second, complementary form — attention on a dilated grid — so every block sees both local and global structure.

blocks.b:
The feature map is decomposed twice. **Block attention** partitions it into $P \times P$ non-overlapping windows and attends within each — Swin's operation, without the shift. **Grid attention** takes a sparse, uniformly spaced $G \times G$ lattice of positions and attends among those, so the participating tokens are spread across the entire image.

Both are implemented as the same primitive on differently reshaped tensors: one gathers a contiguous tile, the other a strided sample. Both have fixed window size, so both are linear in image area, and applying them in sequence gives a block whose receptive field is the whole image at every stage — including the first, which no windowed hierarchy achieves.

Swin's shifted windows propagate information across boundaries over successive layers, so tokens far apart interact only after several blocks, and the rate is set by the window size. Grid attention makes distant interaction immediate: two tokens on opposite sides of the image can be in the same grid group in the very first block.

MaxViT also prefixes each stage with an **MBConv** block — the inverted residual with squeeze-excitation from the MobileNet and EfficientNet line — before the two attention operations. That supplies the local, translation-equivariant mixing that convolution is good at, and its depthwise convolution encodes position implicitly, so no positional embedding is needed. The resulting stage is convolution, then local attention, then global attention, repeated.

MaxViT reports strong results across classification, detection, segmentation and generation, scaling well with both model size and data, and it demonstrates the multi-axis decomposition as a general way to get global receptive field at linear cost.

The constant is large. Three sub-blocks per stage — MBConv, block attention, grid attention — mean more operations and more memory traffic per stage than Swin's two, and the strided gather that grid attention requires is a poor access pattern for hardware that prefers contiguous reads. The design is also, by this point, a deliberate composite: an inverted bottleneck from the efficiency lineage, windowed attention from Swin, and a dilated variant of its own. That the strongest architectures of this period are assemblies rather than single ideas is much the same observation ConvNeXt makes from the convolutional side.

refs.t: MaxViT: Multi-Axis Vision Transformer
Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows

vit>coatnet.lead: ViT generalises better than a convnet given enormous data and worse given ordinary amounts, which is a statement about inductive bias rather than about capacity. CoAtNet's response is not to pick a side but to work out where in a network each bias belongs, and to unify the two operators into one so the choice is principled.

blocks.h: Depthwise convolution and attention, written the same way
blocks.b:
Both operators aggregate over a neighbourhood with weights. Depthwise convolution uses weights $w_{i-j}$ that depend only on the **offset** between positions and are fixed after training; self-attention uses weights $\exp(x_i^\top x_j)$ that depend on the **content** and are recomputed per input.

CoAtNet's relative attention sums the two inside the softmax:

$$y_i = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{G}} \frac{\exp\big(x_i^{\top} x_j + w_{i-j}\big)}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{G}} \exp\big(x_i^{\top} x_k + w_{i-k}\big)} \; x_j$$

so every attention weight carries a learned translation-equivariant prior alongside its content term. This is not a gate choosing between two paths; it is one operator with both properties, and the relative bias is available for free at every layer.

The second contribution is empirical and more consequential. The paper searches over stage layouts — how many convolutional stages before the attention stages begin — and finds a consistent answer: convolution early, attention late.

The reasoning follows from cost and from what each stage needs. Early stages operate at high resolution where global attention is unaffordable and where the useful operations are local anyway. Late stages have few tokens, so attention is cheap, and are where long-range relationships between object parts matter. The C-C-T-T arrangement — two convolutional stages then two transformer stages — generalises better than the alternatives across data regimes, and it is essentially the layout that MaxViT, EfficientFormer and most later hybrids converged on independently.

blocks.h: Good at both ends, distinctive at neither
blocks.b:
CoAtNet was competitive on ImageNet-1k alone and, when pretrained on JFT, took the top of the ImageNet leaderboard at the time — which is the paper's claim, that one family covers the whole data spectrum instead of being tuned for one end.

What it does not do is simplify. The architecture is a composite with a hand-tuned stage layout, and the relative attention adds a bias table to every attention block. The deeper problem the whole hybrid line ran into arrived the following year: ConvNeXt matched Swin using no attention at all, which suggests much of what these architectures were gaining came from macro design and training recipe rather than from the operator — and leaves CoAtNet's careful unification answering a question that turned out to be less decisive than it looked.

refs.t: CoAtNet: Marrying Convolution and Attention for All Data Sizes
An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale

efficientnet>coatnet.lead: CoAtNet's convolutional half is not a generic convnet. Its stages are MBConv blocks — the inverted residual with squeeze-excitation that MobileNet-v2 introduced and EfficientNet's search settled on — chosen because their structure already matches the transformer block they sit beneath.

blocks.h: Why the inverted bottleneck fits under attention
blocks.b:
An MBConv block expands by a factor of four with a $1\times1$, mixes spatially with a depthwise convolution, and projects back down. A transformer's feed-forward network expands by a factor of four with a linear layer and projects back down.

They are the same shape. Both are inverted bottlenecks with a residual across the narrow ends; the difference is that MBConv performs its spatial mixing with a depthwise kernel while the transformer performs it with attention in a separate sublayer. That correspondence is what makes the stages composable — the network's width schedule, normalisation placement and residual structure carry across the convolution-to-attention boundary without adaptation.

blocks.h: Depthwise convolution as the natural partner
blocks.b:
The unification also works because depthwise convolution and attention are the same kind of operation. Both aggregate over positions with a per-channel or per-head weighting and leave cross-channel mixing to the $1\times1$ projections around them.

That is precisely the decoupling Xception argued for and MobileNet made cheap, and it is why relative attention can be written as depthwise convolution's weights added to attention's logits — the two are aggregating the same tensor along the same axis, and only the source of the weights differs.

CoAtNet takes the efficiency lineage's known costs with the block. Depthwise convolutions are memory-bandwidth bound, so the early convolutional stages run below peak on accelerators built for dense matrix multiplication, and squeeze-excitation inserts a global reduction — a synchronisation point — into an otherwise streaming pipeline.

Both are places where measured latency exceeds what the FLOP count implies, and both are the same complaints EfficientNetV2 answered by fusing early depthwise stages back into ordinary convolutions. CoAtNet does not apply that fix, so its convolutional half carries EfficientNet's efficiency profile unchanged — excellent per FLOP, less impressive per millisecond.

refs.t: CoAtNet: Marrying Convolution and Attention for All Data Sizes
EfficientNet: Rethinking Model Scaling for Convolutional Neural Networks
MobileNetV2: Inverted Residuals and Linear Bottlenecks

swin>efficientformer.lead: Swin made attention affordable in FLOPs and left it slow on a phone. EfficientFormer's finding is that most of a vision transformer's mobile latency is not in attention at all — it is in the reshapes, the normalisations and the activations between blocks — and that removing those is worth more than any further attention approximation.

blocks.b:
The paper begins by measuring an actual ViT on an iPhone and attributing the time. Several findings contradict the FLOP-based intuition the field had been designing against.

The patch-embedding convolution with a large kernel and stride is disproportionately expensive. LayerNorm and GELU cost far more than their arithmetic suggests, because they are memory-bound elementwise passes over the whole tensor. And most damaging, the constant conversion between a 4-D tensor layout for convolutional operations and a 3-D token sequence for attention forces reshapes and copies at every boundary — a cost with no FLOPs attached at all.

Attention itself, at the token counts a mobile model uses, is not the bottleneck.

The response is to stop converting. The network runs in 4-D convolutional layout for its early, high-resolution stages, using pooling-based token mixers rather than attention, and switches to 3-D token layout **once**, for the final stage where the grid is small enough that attention is cheap.

One conversion replaces dozens. LayerNorm is replaced by BatchNorm where possible, since BatchNorm folds into the preceding convolution at inference and costs nothing, and GELU by ReLU in the layers where the accuracy difference does not justify the time.

The network's widths and depths are then set by **latency-driven slimming** — a search over per-stage configurations scored against measurements on the target device, in the tradition MnasNet established, rather than against a FLOP budget.

The result is a transformer running at MobileNet-class latency on a phone while retaining ViT-family accuracy, which had not previously been available — the models are not merely FLOP-efficient but fast on hardware.

The qualification is the same one every latency-optimised architecture carries. The profile that motivates the design is one phone, one runtime, one compiler; a different accelerator distributes its time differently, and a runtime that fuses normalisation and activation efficiently removes part of the problem being solved. The design is also frankly a compromise — attention only in the last stage means the global interaction Swin provides throughout is unavailable where the resolution is high, which is exactly where dense prediction needs it.

refs.t: EfficientFormer: Vision Transformers at MobileNet Speed
Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows

mobilenet>efficientformer.lead: EfficientFormer's target is stated as a comparison — a vision transformer that runs as fast as MobileNet on a phone — and it reaches it by adopting the mobile lineage's methods wholesale: measured latency as the objective, depthwise separable stages at high resolution, and a search over per-layer widths.

blocks.h: The benchmark that defines the goal
blocks.b:
MobileNet-v2 on an iPhone is the reference point the paper measures itself against, not a FLOP budget or a parameter count. That choice imports the whole methodology of the mobile line: what counts as success is milliseconds on a named device, and every design decision is justified by a measurement rather than by an operation count.

It also imports the finding that motivated MnasNet. Operations with identical FLOPs differ by large factors in real time, and elementwise operations that barely register in an arithmetic budget — normalisations, activations, layout conversions — can dominate. EfficientFormer's profile of a ViT is the same discovery made on a different architecture.

blocks.h: Depthwise stages where the resolution is high
blocks.b:
The early stages use convolutional token mixers on a 4-D layout — pooling and depthwise convolutions in the MobileNet idiom — precisely because attention at stride 4 is unaffordable on mobile hardware and depthwise separable convolution is what the efficiency lineage established as the cheap alternative.

BatchNorm rather than LayerNorm follows from the same lineage: it folds into the preceding convolution at inference and disappears entirely, which is standard practice in mobile convnets and simply unavailable in a token-layout transformer block.

The latency-driven slimming that sets each stage's width is NetAdapt's procedure, the same fine-grained pass MobileNet-v3 used after its coarse search.

blocks.h: A hybrid, and what that means
blocks.b:
What results is a network that is convolutional where convolution is cheap and attentive where attention is cheap, with one layout change between. It reaches MobileNet-class latency at transformer-class accuracy, which is the intended trade.

The cost is that it is neither thing cleanly. Global interaction is confined to the final stage, so the property that made transformers attractive for dense prediction is absent at the resolutions that need it. And the design is tuned to one device's cost profile, so it inherits the mobile lineage's treadmill — a new accelerator means re-profiling and re-slimming, which is the same constraint MobileNet-v4's universal block was built to loosen.

refs.t: EfficientFormer: Vision Transformers at MobileNet Speed
MobileNets: Efficient Convolutional Neural Networks for Mobile Vision Applications
Searching for MobileNetV3

swin>convnext.lead: Swin beat the convolutional backbones and the field concluded attention was the reason. ConvNeXt tests that by starting from a ResNet-50 and changing one thing at a time — training recipe, macro layout, block structure, kernel size, normalisation — until it matches Swin. No attention is ever added, and it matches.

blocks.b:
The paper is an ablation walk with the accuracy reported after every step, which is what makes it evidence rather than another architecture.

The first step alone is decisive: training ResNet-50 with the modern recipe — 300 epochs, AdamW, RandAugment, mixup, CutMix, random erasing, stochastic depth, label smoothing — lifts it by around two points before any architectural change at all. A substantial part of the reported gap between convnets and transformers was a comparison of a 2016 recipe with a 2021 one.

The remaining steps then modernise the architecture towards Swin's macro design: stage compute ratio changed to $3\!:\!3\!:\!9\!:\!3$ to match Swin's, a patchify stem of a $4\times4$ stride-4 convolution replacing ResNet's $7\times7$ stem and max-pool, and depthwise convolution with a widened base.

Three changes reshape the residual block. The bottleneck is **inverted** — narrow, wide, narrow with a $4\times$ expansion — matching both MobileNet-v2 and the transformer's feed-forward proportions.

The depthwise kernel is enlarged to $7 \times 7$ and **moved before** the expansion, so the expensive spatial operation runs at the narrow width. This is the analogue of attention preceding the MLP in a transformer block, and $7\times7$ is Swin's window size — the paper reports accuracy rising with kernel size up to about there and then flattening.

The micro-level changes reduce the block's furniture: GELU instead of ReLU, a **single** activation and a **single** normalisation per block rather than one after every convolution, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, and separate downsampling layers between stages. Fewer normalisations and activations is itself worth accuracy, and it is exactly what a transformer block already looks like.

blocks.h: What it shows, and what it does not
blocks.b:
ConvNeXt matches or beats Swin across ImageNet, COCO and ADE20K at comparable FLOPs, and does so with a pure convolutional network that is simpler to implement and faster on most hardware — no windowing, no shifts, no attention masks.

The conclusion is careful. It does not show attention is useless; it shows that the 2020–21 gains attributed to attention were substantially due to macro design and training protocol, and that a convnet given both is competitive. Attention retains properties convolution does not have — input-dependent, unbounded-range interaction — which matter for the multimodal and generative settings where transformers remained dominant regardless. The pure convolutional form also gives up the transformer's easy compatibility with masked-token pretraining, which is the gap ConvNeXt-v2 had to engineer around.

refs.t: A ConvNet for the 2020s
Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows

resnet>convnext.lead: ConvNeXt's starting point is not an abstraction — it is ResNet-50, with its weights, its stage structure and its published accuracy. Every step in the paper is measured against that baseline, which is what lets it separate what the residual network was missing from what convolution itself could not do.

blocks.b:
The skeleton survives intact. Four stages at strides 4, 8, 16 and 32; residual connections throughout; a linear classifier on global average pooling. ConvNeXt is a ResNet in the sense that a reader of the 2016 paper would recognise the diagram.

What this means for the comparison is that the two networks differ in a list of enumerable changes rather than in kind. The paper can therefore attribute accuracy to each change, and the total is the sum of a dozen small decisions rather than a single idea.

The most-cited number in the paper is the one before any architecture is touched. ResNet-50 trained with the modern protocol — AdamW, 300 epochs, RandAugment, mixup, CutMix, random erasing, stochastic depth, label smoothing — gains roughly two points over its published figure.

That single result recontextualises several years of comparisons. Architectures introduced between 2019 and 2021 were routinely compared against ResNet's original numbers, so part of every reported advantage was the training protocol rather than the design. It is a caution that applies well beyond this arrow: ResNeSt, the EfficientNet family and the early ViT results all mix architecture and recipe in their headline figures.

blocks.h: The changes, in order of size
blocks.b:
After the recipe, the significant steps are the stage compute ratio, the patchify stem, depthwise convolution with a wider base, the inverted bottleneck, the large depthwise kernel moved ahead of the expansion, and the micro-level simplifications — GELU, one activation and one normalisation per block, LayerNorm, separate downsampling layers.

Each is individually worth a fraction of a point and none is novel; every one is borrowed from ResNeXt, MobileNet-v2, Swin or the transformer block. The claim is about the aggregate, and about what it implies: the gap between a 2016 convnet and a 2021 transformer was a decade of accumulated small conventions, not a change in what the operator could represent.

The cost of the finding is that ConvNeXt is not itself a new idea, which the authors state plainly. And LayerNorm over a convolutional feature map is a slightly awkward object — it is what the transformer block uses, adopted for consistency rather than derived, and it does not fold into the preceding convolution the way BatchNorm does.

refs.t: A ConvNet for the 2020s
Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

convnext>convnext2.lead: Masked autoencoding had become the standard way to pretrain a vision transformer, and applying it to ConvNeXt gave almost nothing. ConvNeXt-v2 diagnoses why — the architecture's features collapse under the objective — and fixes it with a normalisation that forces channels to compete.

blocks.h: Why masking is awkward for a convnet
blocks.b:
A transformer can simply drop masked tokens: MAE's encoder processes only the visible quarter of patches, which is where its speed comes from. A convolution has no such option, since it slides over a dense grid and a hole in that grid is not something it can skip.

The **fully convolutional masked autoencoder** treats the masked input as a sparse tensor and uses sparse convolutions during pretraining, so masked regions genuinely contribute nothing rather than being filled with a learned token that the network can come to rely on. At fine-tuning time the same weights run as ordinary dense convolutions. The decoder is deliberately minimal — a single ConvNeXt block — since the paper finds a heavier decoder does not help.

blocks.h: Feature collapse, and the response normalisation
blocks.b:
With that in place the results were still disappointing, and the diagnosis came from inspecting activations: many channels were nearly duplicates of one another. Under a reconstruction objective there is little pressure for channels to differentiate, and the network settles into a redundant representation.

**Global Response Normalization** makes channels compete. It aggregates each channel to a scalar by an $L_2$ norm over the spatial extent, divides by the mean of those norms across channels, and uses the result to calibrate the channel:

$$\hat{X}_i = X_i \cdot \frac{\|X_i\|}{\frac{1}{C}\sum_{j=1}^{C}\|X_j\|}$$

A channel with a below-average response is scaled down and one above average scaled up, so channels are measured against each other rather than normalised in isolation. Added to the block with a residual and two learned parameters, this is what makes the pretraining pay: the paper reports the architecture change and the pretraining being largely useless apart and clearly effective together.

The result is a family from tiny to huge in which self-supervised pretraining improves ConvNeXt as reliably as MAE improves a ViT, closing the last practical advantage transformers held for pretraining at scale.

The paper's own framing — that the architecture and the pretraining objective had to be designed together — is the interesting part and also the limitation. GRN is a fix for a failure mode of one objective on one architecture; it is not a general normalisation with an independent justification, and its benefit outside this pairing is modest. The sparse-convolution pretraining path also requires kernels that not every framework provides efficiently, which is friction a transformer's token-dropping does not have.

refs.t: ConvNeXt V2: Co-designing and Scaling ConvNets with Masked Autoencoders
A ConvNet for the 2020s

mae>convnext2.lead: MAE showed that masking most of an image and reconstructing it is a strong pretraining signal — for a transformer, whose encoder can simply skip the masked tokens. Carrying that to a convolutional network required rebuilding the mechanism, because a convolution cannot skip anything.

blocks.b:
MAE's efficiency comes from an asymmetry: the encoder sees only the visible $25\%$ of patches, and mask tokens are introduced in a lightweight decoder. That is possible because a transformer operates on a set, so removing elements is free.

A convolution operates on a grid. Deleting positions is not defined, and the usual substitutes are both unsatisfactory — filling masked regions with a constant leaks the mask pattern into every layer through the receptive field, and using a learned fill token gives the network something to detect rather than something to ignore. Neither reproduces MAE's clean separation between what the encoder sees and what it must predict.

FCMAE treats the masked image as a **sparse tensor** and uses sparse convolutions, which compute only at visible positions and propagate the sparsity pattern through the encoder. Masked regions contribute nothing at any depth, which is the property MAE gets for free.

The same weights then run as ordinary dense convolutions when fine-tuning, so no architectural divergence between pretraining and downstream use is introduced. The high mask ratio MAE established — around $60\%$ here, with the paper noting convolutional models prefer a somewhat lower ratio than ViT's $75\%$ — carries over, as does the principle that the difficulty of the task is what makes the representation useful.

blocks.h: The objective needed the architecture changed too
blocks.b:
Transplanting the mechanism was necessary and not sufficient. ConvNeXt under FCMAE alone performed poorly, and the reason was feature collapse — channels becoming redundant because a reconstruction objective applies no pressure for them to differentiate. GRN was added to make channels compete, and only the pair works.

That is the substantive finding of this arrow. A pretraining objective is not architecture-neutral: MAE was developed against a ViT and quietly relies on properties of it, and moving it to another family meant both re-implementing the masking and modifying the network to survive the objective. The generative-pretraining idea travelled; the specific recipe did not.

refs.t: Masked Autoencoders Are Scalable Vision Learners
ConvNeXt V2: Co-designing and Scaling ConvNets with Masked Autoencoders

vit>mae.lead: ViT's weakness was that it needed hundreds of millions of labelled images to beat a convnet. MAE removes the labels: mask three quarters of the patches, reconstruct the missing pixels, and use the encoder afterwards. What makes it practical rather than merely possible is an asymmetry — the encoder never sees the masked patches at all.

blocks.h: Why masking works here and not in vision generally
blocks.b:
BERT's masked language modelling had been the standard pretraining objective in NLP for years, and vision attempts to copy it had underwhelmed. He et al. name three reasons, and the interesting one is about information density.

Language is dense: a masked word is often recoverable only by understanding the sentence. Images are highly redundant, so a masked patch can usually be interpolated from its neighbours without understanding anything. The response is to raise the mask ratio far past NLP's $15\%$ — to $75\%$ — so that local interpolation is unavailable and reconstruction requires a global sense of what the scene contains.

The second reason is architectural, and had only just been removed: a convolutional network cannot naturally process a partial input, which is precisely the problem ConvNeXt-v2 later had to solve with sparse convolutions. ViT can, because it operates on a set of tokens.

The encoder runs on the **visible $25\%$ only**. No mask tokens are introduced, so it processes a quarter of the sequence, and since attention is quadratic the saving is larger than fourfold — the paper reports around a threefold speedup with lower memory, which is what makes pretraining a ViT-Huge affordable.

Mask tokens enter in a **lightweight decoder**, shallow and narrow, which sees the encoded visible patches plus a shared learned mask token at each missing position, with positional embeddings supplying the geometry. The decoder is discarded after pretraining.

The target is pixels — the paper finds reconstructing per-patch normalised pixel values works better than raw ones — which is deliberately simpler than BEiT's route through a separately trained dVAE tokeniser. The decoder's asymmetry is what allows such a naive target: because the decoder is small and thrown away, the encoder is not obliged to keep the low-level detail needed to render the output.

MAE fine-tunes to strong ImageNet accuracy from ImageNet-1k alone, removing ViT's dependence on a proprietary labelled corpus, and it scales cleanly — the larger the model, the more the pretraining is worth. It became the default initialisation for large vision transformers, including SAM's image encoder.

The representation is nonetheless better suited to fine-tuning than to being used frozen: MAE's linear-probe accuracy trails contrastive methods like CLIP and DINO, because a reconstruction objective preserves detail that a linear classifier cannot exploit, where a contrastive objective produces a more linearly separable space by construction. And the whole approach is tied to token-based architectures, which is the gap ConvNeXt-v2 was written to close.

refs.t: Masked Autoencoders Are Scalable Vision Learners
BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
BEiT: BERT Pre-Training of Image Transformers

convnext>inceptionnext.lead: ConvNeXt's $7 \times 7$ depthwise kernel is central to its accuracy and unhelpfully slow — a large depthwise convolution performs very little arithmetic per byte it moves, so it runs far below what its FLOP count suggests. InceptionNeXt keeps the large effective kernel and decomposes it so that most channels never touch it.

blocks.h: A cheap operation that is not fast
blocks.b:
Depthwise convolution applies one kernel per channel and does no cross-channel mixing, so its arithmetic intensity — operations per byte of memory traffic — is low. The kernel is memory-bandwidth bound, and enlarging it from $3\times3$ to $7\times7$ raises the FLOPs modestly while the time cost rises much more than proportionally on hardware built for dense matrix multiplication.

The result is that ConvNeXt's large-kernel block accounts for a small share of the network's FLOPs and a large share of its latency. Any fix that merely reduces FLOPs is aiming at the wrong quantity.

blocks.h: Splitting the channels, not just the kernel
blocks.b:
InceptionNeXt divides the block's channels into four groups and applies a different, cheaper operation to each: a small $3\times3$ square kernel, a $1 \times k$ horizontal band, a $k \times 1$ vertical band, and an **identity** — a group that is passed through untouched.

The two orthogonal bands are what preserve the large receptive field: a $1\times11$ followed in effect by an $11\times1$ across parallel branches spans an $11 \times 11$ region using $22$ weights rather than $121$, the same factorisation Inception-v3 applied to its own kernels. The identity branch is the blunter economy — a substantial fraction of channels simply skip the spatial operation, and the paper's ablation finds accuracy is largely insensitive to that, which says the dense large kernel was doing redundant work.

The result is a block with ConvNeXt's effective receptive field, measurably higher throughput, and comparable accuracy.

The decomposition is not free in what it can express. A dense $k \times k$ kernel can represent any correlation within its window; a pair of orthogonal bands plus a small square cannot represent a diagonal structure at full extent, and the identity branch contributes no spatial mixing at all. The effective receptive field is preserved along the axes and thinned elsewhere.

What the result argues is that this loss is cheap — that the accuracy of a large kernel comes mostly from its reach along the principal axes, not from dense coverage. It also brings the Inception idea back after it had been abandoned as an architecture: parallel branches of differing extent, fused by concatenation, but now inside one block of an otherwise uniform network rather than as the organising principle of the whole design.

refs.t: InceptionNeXt: When Inception Meets ConvNeXt
A ConvNet for the 2020s

inceptionv3>inceptionnext.lead: Inception's two enduring ideas — parallel branches of different extent, and factorising an $n \times n$ kernel into $n \times 1$ and $1 \times n$ — were abandoned along with the architecture that carried them. InceptionNeXt revives both, at the scale of a single block inside a network that is otherwise uniform.

blocks.b:
Inception-v3's asymmetric factorisation replaced an $n \times n$ convolution with a $n \times 1$ followed by a $1 \times n$, cutting the weight count from $n^2$ to $2n$ and the arithmetic in proportion. The paper was careful about where it applied — helpful on medium-sized grids, unhelpful early in the network.

InceptionNeXt uses the same decomposition on a depthwise kernel and arranges the two bands as **parallel branches** rather than in series. A $1 \times 11$ and an $11 \times 1$ acting on different channel groups span an $11 \times 11$ extent for $22$ weights, which is the economy Inception identified, now applied to the large-kernel design ConvNeXt had established.

The other inheritance is the module shape. An Inception module splits its input across branches with different receptive fields and concatenates the results, so one block sees several scales without committing to a kernel size. InceptionNeXt's four groups — small square, two bands, identity — are exactly that construction.

The difference is scope. Inception made this the organising principle of the entire network, with each module hand-designed and each stage different, which is what made the family untunable and eventually indefensible. InceptionNeXt confines it to one block that is then repeated uniformly, so the architecture keeps ConvNeXt's regularity and stage structure while the multi-scale idea lives inside a single token mixer.

The motivation moved. Inception's branches existed to enrich the representation — several scales at once, more expressive than one kernel. InceptionNeXt's exist to make a known-good large kernel run faster, and its identity branch, which contributes nothing representationally, is the clearest sign of that: it is there because skipping the spatial operation on some channels costs little accuracy and saves real time.

So the same construction is being used for the opposite reason, which is a reasonable summary of what changed in convolutional design between 2016 and 2024. Capacity stopped being the scarce resource and memory bandwidth became it, and the shapes that were introduced to add expressiveness were rediscovered as ways to remove traffic.

refs.t: InceptionNeXt: When Inception Meets ConvNeXt
Rethinking the Inception Architecture for Computer Vision

unet>ddpm.lead: A diffusion model needs a network that maps a noisy image to a prediction at the same resolution, conditioned on how noisy it is. That is exactly U-Net's shape, and DDPM takes it essentially unmodified — the generative line's central architecture is borrowed wholesale from medical image segmentation.

blocks.b:
DDPM trains a network $\epsilon_\theta$ to predict the noise added to an image, minimising

$$\mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, \epsilon}\Big[\big\|\epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon,\; t)\big\|^2\Big]$$

The input is an image and the output is an image of identical size. Sampling runs the network hundreds of times, so it must also be affordable.

U-Net answers both. Its contracting path builds global context — necessary, because the noise to remove at one pixel depends on what the whole image is becoming — and its expanding path with concatenating skips restores full resolution with detail preserved. An encoder-only network could not produce a full-resolution output; a network without downsampling could not see globally at acceptable cost.

Three modifications adapt it. The timestep $t$ is encoded with a sinusoidal embedding — the Transformer's positional encoding, reused for a scalar — passed through a small MLP and injected into every residual block, so one network serves every noise level rather than needing one model per step.

Self-attention blocks are inserted at the lower-resolution stages, where the token count is small enough to afford them, supplying the long-range coherence that convolution alone struggles with over a full image. And group normalisation replaces batch normalisation, since sampling has no meaningful batch statistics.

The skips do something subtly different here from in segmentation. In U-Net they carry spatial detail that pooling discarded; in a denoiser they also carry the high-frequency content of the noisy input itself, which the network needs because it is predicting a residual rather than synthesising from scratch.

The U-Net denoiser held for years — improved in Ho and Nichol's follow-ups, scaled in the diffusion-beats-GANs work, moved into a compressed latent space by Stable Diffusion, but structurally the same network.

Its limitations are the ones that eventually displaced it. The architecture is a pile of hand-set choices — which resolutions get attention, how many blocks per level, channel multipliers per stage — with no scaling law relating them to compute. And convolution's locality means global consistency depends on those few attention layers at the coarse levels. DiT replaces the whole thing with a plain transformer over latent patches, and shows FID improving predictably with compute, which is the property the U-Net never offered.

vit>dit.lead: Diffusion models had inherited the U-Net from DDPM and kept it for years, tuning it by hand with no principle relating its size to its quality. DiT replaces it with a Vision Transformer over latent patches and demonstrates the property the U-Net never had: sample quality improving predictably as compute is added.

blocks.b:
Operating in a VAE's latent space, DiT patchifies the latent into tokens exactly as ViT patchifies an image, adds positional embeddings, and runs a standard transformer stack. There is no downsampling, no skip connections, and no convolution — the sequence length is set once by the patch size and stays fixed.

The patch size is the compute knob. Halving it quadruples the token count and therefore the FLOPs, at unchanged parameter count, and the paper finds sample quality tracks **FLOPs** rather than parameters — a smaller model at a finer patch size beats a larger one at a coarse patch size. That is the scaling relationship the field wanted and could not extract from a U-Net, whose depth, width, attention placement and channel schedule interact in ways no single number captures.

Conditioning on the timestep and class label is where the design work is. The paper compares in-context tokens, cross-attention, and adaptive layer normalisation, and finds a specific variant of the last clearly best.

Adaptive LayerNorm regresses the scale and shift of each normalisation from the conditioning vector rather than learning them as free parameters. **adaLN-Zero** adds a third regressed parameter — a gate $\alpha$ scaling each residual branch — and initialises the layer producing it to zero:

$$x \leftarrow x + \alpha \cdot \mathrm{Attention}\big(\gamma \cdot \mathrm{LN}(x) + \beta\big)$$

so every block begins as the exact identity and its contribution grows only as training finds a use for it. This is the residual-scaling idea that Inception-ResNet needed for stability, made learned and per-block, and the paper reports it markedly better than plain adaLN. It also costs the least compute of the options considered, since conditioning enters through normalisation parameters rather than through extra attention.

DiT set the state of the art on class-conditional ImageNet generation and, more consequentially, established the transformer as the diffusion backbone. Stable Diffusion 3 and the video models that followed are built on this architecture rather than on a U-Net, and Sora's spacetime patches are the same construction extended over time.

The costs are the transformer's. Attention is quadratic in token count, so fine patch sizes are expensive and high-resolution generation depends on the latent space being small — DiT is not a pixel-space model. Training is also slower to converge than a U-Net at equal compute, which is the usual price for removing an inductive bias, and it is affordable here only because the scaling behaviour makes the additional compute worth spending.

alexnet>dqn.lead: Reinforcement learning had worked from hand-engineered state features, because nobody could make a function approximator stable enough to learn a value function from raw sensory input. DQN puts an AlexNet-style convolutional stack in front of Q-learning and adds two mechanisms that make the combination converge.

blocks.h: The perception problem, and the borrowed answer
blocks.b:
Classical value-based RL assumed a compact state description supplied by a person. Applied to Atari, that meant hand-coded features per game, and the agent's competence was largely the feature designer's.

DQN takes the screen instead — four stacked greyscale frames, downsampled — and passes it through a convolutional network of the kind AlexNet had established: a few convolutional layers with ReLU, then a fully connected head, with the output being one $Q$-value per action rather than a class distribution. The same weights and the same architecture are used for every game, with only the action count differing, which is the result that made the paper famous: one learner, no per-task feature engineering.

blocks.h: Why it does not converge naively
blocks.b:
Combining $Q$-learning with a nonlinear approximator was known to diverge, for two reasons that DQN addresses separately.

**Experience replay.** Consecutive frames are almost identical, so online updates are made on highly correlated samples — a violation of the independence that stochastic gradient descent assumes, and one that lets the network overwrite what it learned a moment ago. Transitions are stored in a buffer and sampled uniformly at random, which decorrelates the updates and reuses each experience many times.

**A target network.** The regression target $r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')$ is computed from the network being updated, so every gradient step moves the target — the network chases its own output. DQN keeps a frozen copy $Q^-$, updated every few thousand steps, and regresses towards

$$y = r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^{-}(s', a')$$

so the target is stationary between refreshes.

Reward clipping to $[-1, 1]$ lets one learning rate serve games with wildly different score scales — a practical necessity, and one that flattens genuine differences in reward magnitude.

DQN reached human-level or better play on a majority of the Atari suite from pixels alone, and it is the point at which deep learning entered reinforcement learning as the default rather than as an experiment. Everything in the RL lane after it assumes a learned perceptual front end.

The convolutional stack itself was never the difficulty — it is a smaller and simpler network than AlexNet, and it worked. What was hard was everything the transplant destabilised, and the immediate successors are all corrections to that: Double DQN for the $\max$ operator's overestimation bias, prioritised replay for uniform sampling's inefficiency, and duelling architectures for the value-advantage decomposition the single head conflates.

alexnet>showtell.lead: Image captioning had been a pipeline of detectors, attribute classifiers and template filling. Show and Tell replaces it with an encoder-decoder: a convolutional network summarises the image into a vector, and a recurrent language model is conditioned on that vector and generates the sentence.

blocks.h: The image as the first word
blocks.b:
The construction is borrowed directly from neural machine translation, where an encoder RNN compresses a source sentence to a vector and a decoder RNN generates the target from it. Vinyals et al. replace the source encoder with a CNN:

$$\theta^{\star} = \arg\max_{\theta} \sum_{(I, S)} \log p(S \mid I; \theta), \qquad \log p(S \mid I) = \sum_{t} \log p(S_t \mid I, S_0, \ldots, S_{t-1})$$

with an LSTM modelling the conditional. The image embedding is fed in **once**, as the input at the first timestep, before the sentence tokens begin.

Feeding it only once is a deliberate choice the paper ablates: supplying the image at every step performed worse, overfitting to visual noise. So the LSTM's state must carry the entire image representation through the whole generation, which is an information bottleneck by construction.

blocks.h: Features that were never trained for this
blocks.b:
The CNN is an ImageNet classifier, and the paper's finding is that a representation learned for assigning one of a thousand labels contains enough to describe a scene in a sentence.

The practical detail is what to freeze. Captioning datasets are small relative to ImageNet, so fine-tuning the whole convolutional stack overfits — the authors keep it fixed initially and fine-tune only late and carefully. That the transfer works at all is the same claim R-CNN made for detection, extended into a different modality: classification pretraining had become the general-purpose visual front end for any task.

blocks.h: The bottleneck, and what replaced it
blocks.b:
A single fixed-length vector must represent everything about the image that any part of the sentence might mention. Describing a specific object in a cluttered scene requires detail that a global pooled feature has already averaged away, and the model shows this — captions that are fluent, plausible and unspecific, often reciting a common configuration rather than what is present.

The fix arrived quickly and from the same place as the original architecture. **Show, Attend and Tell** lets the decoder attend over a spatial grid of CNN features, choosing what to look at as it produces each word, which is Bahdanau attention transplanted into vision-language. That line runs directly to the transformer-based captioners, and then to CLIP, which discards the generative decoder entirely and aligns images with text contrastively instead.

vit>clip.lead: CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder to agree, so that a picture and its caption land near each other in one embedding space. The image tower is a Vision Transformer, and the pairing matters in both directions — the ViT gives CLIP a scalable encoder, and CLIP gives the ViT a training signal that does not require labels.

blocks.b:
ViT's stated requirement was a labelled corpus of a size only a few organisations possessed. CLIP's observation is that image-text pairs are abundant on the web and require no annotation effort, and that a caption is a richer target than a class index — it names objects, relations, attributes and context.

Training maximises the cosine similarity of matched pairs against all mismatched pairs in the batch, symmetrically in both directions, with a learned temperature. The batch is the source of negatives, so the objective sharpens as the batch grows — CLIP's are very large for this reason. Around 400 million pairs supply the scale the architecture wanted, from a source that needed no labelling.

blocks.h: Why a transformer on both sides
blocks.b:
Using the same family for image and text is what makes the system uniform: two towers, each producing one embedding, joined only by a dot product. There is no fusion module and no cross-attention, which is what keeps inference cheap — image embeddings can be computed once and cached, and a text query is a single forward pass and a matrix multiply.

The paper compares ResNet and ViT image towers and finds the transformer more compute-efficient at scale, which is consistent with ViT's own finding that its advantage appears once data is plentiful. CLIP's regime is exactly that, so the architecture is being used where its trade is favourable.

blocks.h: Zero-shot, and what it rests on
blocks.b:
Because the text tower can embed any string, classification needs no training: embed the candidate class names as prompts, embed the image, take the nearest. CLIP matched a fully supervised ResNet-50 on ImageNet without seeing a single ImageNet training example, and was substantially more robust on the distribution-shifted variants where supervised models collapse.

The consequences run beyond classification. The CLIP text encoder became the conditioning signal for text-to-image generation — Stable Diffusion's cross-attention reads it — and the image tower became a standard visual front end for multimodal language models.

The costs are real. Performance depends on prompt wording, which makes evaluation slippery; the model inherits whatever associations the uncurated web supplies, which the paper documents at length; and it is weak on tasks with no natural caption description, such as counting or fine-grained discrimination between classes that are rarely named precisely. Contrastive alignment also gives a space that is good for retrieval and comparison and does not by itself support generation — which is why the multimodal line needed a generative decoder attached on top.

refs.t: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale

vit>sora.lead: ViT's contribution was a way to turn an image into a sequence of tokens that a transformer can consume without any vision-specific machinery. Sora extends the cut into time — patches become **spacetime patches** carved from a compressed video latent — and inherits with it the ability to handle any duration, resolution or aspect ratio in one model.

blocks.b:
ViT divides an image into a grid of non-overlapping patches and flattens them into a sequence, which makes the transformer indifferent to the two-dimensional structure it came from. The same move applied to video takes blocks that extend across space **and** time, so each token summarises a small region over a short interval.

Sora runs this on a learned compressed latent rather than on pixels — a video encoder reduces the raw frames spatially and temporally first, and patches are extracted from that. This is the latent-diffusion economy applied to video, and it is what keeps the token count manageable when the third dimension multiplies it.

A convolutional video model with a fixed architecture wants a fixed frame count and resolution, so training data is cropped and resized to a canonical form and generation produces that form.

A sequence of patches has no such constraint: a longer or larger video is simply more tokens. Training can therefore use videos at their native resolution, aspect ratio and duration, and the reported effect is not merely convenience — models trained on native aspect ratios frame their subjects better than models trained on square crops, because square-cropped training data teaches the model that subjects are centred and partially cut off.

The underlying generator is a diffusion transformer in DiT's mould, denoising patch tokens, so the scaling behaviour DiT demonstrated for images carries over: sample quality improves with training compute in a way the U-Net-based video models did not offer.

blocks.h: What the tokens do not contain
blocks.b:
Sora produces long, temporally coherent, high-resolution video, and the emergent behaviours reported — rough object permanence, consistent occlusion, some simulation of interaction — are properties nobody built in.

They are also unreliable, and the failure modes point at what the representation lacks. Physical plausibility is learned as a statistical regularity of video, not as a constraint, so objects deform, merge, or violate causality in ways that are locally smooth and globally wrong. Long-range consistency is bounded by the context the attention can span. And the cost is severe: attention is quadratic in token count and a video's token count is large even after latent compression, which is why generation is far from real time and why the model exists at a scale few can reproduce.

sam>sam2.lead: SAM made a mask the answer to a prompt rather than a lookup in a fixed class list, but every answer stood alone: click a fish in one frame and the model knows nothing about the next. SAM 2 keeps the promptable decoder almost unchanged and inserts a memory between frames, so what was segmented once conditions everything segmented after.

blocks.b:
SAM's contribution was an interface. A prompt becomes a few tokens if it is a point or a box, or — if it is a coarse mask — a convolutional embedding added element-wise to the image embedding, and a two-layer decoder cross-attends those tokens against an image embedding computed once, so each further prompt costs milliseconds rather than a fresh encoder pass. Because a point is ambiguous — the strap, the bag, the person carrying it — the decoder returns several masks with scores, and training supervises only the best of them. Around that sat a data engine: annotators corrected model output, the corrections retrained the model, and the loop tightened until most masks needed no correction at all, yielding SA-1B.

Two pieces of this are reusable rather than specific. The decoder is indifferent to where its image embedding came from or what conditioned it. And the annotation loop is a recipe, not a one-off, provided the model inside it is fast enough for a person to work against in real time.

blocks.h: Conditioning a frame on the past
blocks.b:
SAM 2 keeps the prompt encoder, the ambiguity-aware decoder and the encode-once asymmetry, and discards the assumption that frames are independent. A memory encoder fuses each predicted mask with its own frame embedding into a spatial memory; a memory bank holds the recent frames together with the frames the user actually prompted; and memory attention lets the current frame's embedding cross-attend to those memories before the decoder ever sees it. Alongside the spatial memories sit object pointers — compact vectors taken from the decoder's output token, carrying what the object is rather than where it last was.

Two additions are forced by the removal. An object can leave the frame entirely, so the decoder gains an occlusion head that predicts whether the target is present at all; a still-image model never had to say no. And SAM's ViT-H gives way to a hierarchical MAE-pretrained backbone, because a model that runs on every frame of a stream cannot carry that encoder cost.

blocks.h: What it bought, and the drift
blocks.b:
Annotation was the immediate return: with SAM 2 in the loop, masking a video ran far faster than frame-by-frame use of SAM, which is what made the SA-V corpus — tens of thousands of videos, tens of millions of masks — collectable at all, and interactive video segmentation reached comparable accuracy from markedly fewer clicks. The less expected return was on still images, where SAM 2 is both more accurate than SAM and several times faster.

The cost sits in the memory. The bank is a recent window plus the prompted frames, so identity survives a brief occlusion and drifts through a long one, with no re-identification once the thread is lost — only another click. Multiple objects are tracked by running separate memories over a shared image embedding, so the model never reasons about them jointly. And a mask still comes back without a name.
